ARCHITECTURE.md.overview: The contributor-facing architecture guide. It maps the end-to-end pipeline from the WebUI/CLI through the LangGraph `TradingAgentsGraph` to Alpaca execution, lists which package owns which responsibility, and documents where every run persists data. It is the natural second stop of the Project Overview tour step, after the README sells the features.

sections.title: Big-picture pipeline diagram
sections.explanation: An ASCII diagram shows the three phases inside the graph: five parallel analysts, the bull/bear research debate judged by a research manager, and the execution chain (trader, risky/safe/neutral risk debate, risk manager). The closing paragraph stresses that final decisions are executable actions (`BUY/HOLD/SELL` or `LONG/NEUTRAL/SHORT`) carried in a typed `TradeIntent`, and that only numeric stop-loss/take-profit values become broker-side bracket/OTO orders.

sections.title: Package map
sections.explanation: A table pairs each directory with its job. Note how `tradingagents/graph/` is split into small single-purpose modules (`setup.py` wires nodes, `conditional_logic.py` routes debates, `propagation.py` builds initial state), which is exactly the cluster of files covered in the Graph Orchestration tour step. It also names `default_config.py` as the single source of defaults and `dataflows/config.py` as the runtime config plus API key holder.

sections.title: Analysis lifecycle
sections.explanation: Six numbered stages describe one `propagate(symbol, date)` call: kickoff with an immediately opened run log, analysts, research debate, execution chain, signal extraction and optional auto-execution, and finally the decision log entry. The last bullet carries an important caveat: resolved outcomes are hypothetical fixed-horizon asset returns, not broker fill-based profits.

sections.title: Memory and persistence
sections.explanation: Explains the two complementary memories: the markdown `TradingMemoryLog` of every final decision, and five ChromaDB `FinancialSituationMemory` collections keyed by situation embedding. The persistence table is a handy reference for where audit logs, the decision log, safety state (including the `KILL_SWITCH` flag), caches, and SQLite checkpoints live on disk.

sections.title: Configuration and testing rules
sections.explanation: Restates that config flows from `default_config.py` with per-run overrides and keys from `.env`, and warns to keep `ALPACA_USE_PAPER=True` while developing. The testing conventions (deterministic, no network, mocked boundaries, import-time no-network guards) explain why the test suite can pass on a fresh clone.

sections.title: Integrated contribution set
sections.explanation: A changelog-style table of the stacked pull requests that were merged together: risk sizing, backtesting, self-learning memory, bracket orders, the safety layer, CI, regime detection, alerts, and more. It is useful for tracing why a given subsystem exists and which PR introduced it.

QUICKSTART.md.overview: A five-minute onboarding path from clone to first analysis. It covers installation, the minimum `.env` keys, launching the Dash WebUI or CLI, verifying with the test suite, where results are stored, and common troubleshooting. It belongs to the Project Overview tour step as the most practical entry document.

sections.title: Install
sections.explanation: Standard clone, virtualenv, and `pip install -r requirements.txt` steps, with separate activation commands for Windows and macOS/Linux.

sections.title: Configure keys
sections.explanation: Shows copying `env.sample` to `.env` and a table separating required keys (Alpaca key/secret and an LLM provider key) from optional data providers such as Finnhub, FRED, FXMacroData, and CoinDesk. The callout to keep `ALPACA_USE_PAPER=True` mirrors the safety stance repeated across the project's docs.

sections.title: Run and verify
sections.explanation: The WebUI (`python run_webui_dash.py`) is the primary path; the CLI (`python -m cli.main`) runs the same pipeline interactively. Running `python -m pytest tests/` is presented as a setup check because the suite needs no network or live keys.

sections.title: Results and troubleshooting
sections.explanation: Points to the per-run audit trail under `eval_results/` and the decision log under `~/.tradingagents/memory/`. The troubleshooting table captures frequent failures such as missing keys, live keys used against the paper API, rate-limit stalls, and using `BTCUSD` instead of the required slash format `BTC/USD`.

README.md.overview: The project's front page. It positions AlpacaTradingAgent as an independent, Alpaca-focused extension of the Tauric Research TradingAgents framework, lists its features (Alpaca execution, stocks plus crypto, five analysts, multi-provider LLMs, structured decisions, scheduling, Dash UI), and documents installation, API keys, CLI/WebUI/Docker usage, prompt customization, and Python package usage. It is the first document in the Project Overview tour step.

sections.title: Intro and disclaimer
sections.explanation: Introduces the project, credits the original TradingAgents framework, and includes a disclaimer that it is for education and research, not financial advice. Navigation links point to QUICKSTART.md and ARCHITECTURE.md for deeper reading.

sections.title: Enhanced features
sections.explanation: Feature bullets grouped by theme. Worth noting: the five-analyst team (adding a FRED-backed Macro analyst), structured outputs with free-text fallback, advisory ratings that never directly trigger orders, checkpoint resume, safe ticker paths (`BTC/USD -> BTC_USD`), and default position sizing caps. These features correspond to later tour steps on LLM providers, structured decisions, and risk sizing.

sections.title: Framework roles
sections.explanation: Describes the agent teams that mirror a trading firm: analysts, bull/bear researchers, a trader, and risk management/portfolio manager. This is the conceptual model that `AgentState` and the graph routing implement.

sections.title: Installation and API keys
sections.explanation: Lists every supported key grouped by purpose: essential Alpaca and OpenAI keys, per-provider LLM keys (selected via `LLM_PROVIDER`), financial, macro, and crypto data APIs, and the optional runtime path overrides. Without valid Alpaca keys the app falls back to a demo mode without trading.

sections.title: CLI, WebUI, Docker, and prompts
sections.explanation: Documents `python -m cli.main`, the Dash launcher's flags, the Docker Compose path with `HOST_PORT`, and how to override Markdown prompt templates via `TRADINGAGENTS_PROMPT_DIR` while keeping the same group path.

sections.title: Web UI feature tour
sections.explanation: A visual walkthrough (GIFs) of the multi-symbol dashboard, live trading integration, charts, tabbed reports, scheduled auto-trading, and LLM runtime controls in the WebUI.

sections.title: Python package usage
sections.explanation: Shows programmatic use: build `TradingAgentsGraph` with `DEFAULT_CONFIG.copy()` and call `propagate(symbol, date)`. The custom-config example is a compact tour of the most important config keys (model choices, per-model reasoning params, debate rounds, `allow_shorts`, checkpointing, and analyst delays) that are defined in `default_config.py`.

sections.title: Contributing and citation
sections.explanation: Points to the Postman API check setup, acknowledges the upstream project, and provides the BibTeX citation for the original TradingAgents paper.

env.sample.overview: The template for the `.env` file that `tradingagents/dataflows/config.py` loads with `python-dotenv`. It documents every environment variable the project reads: runtime paths, LLM provider selection, OpenAI and local OpenAI-compatible settings, keys for other LLM providers and Azure, and trading/market/news/macro data keys. It is part of the Central Configuration tour step.

sections.title: Usage instructions
sections.explanation: Header comments explain the copy-to-`.env` workflow, the need to restart after edits, and the warning to keep paper trading on unless live trading is intended.

sections.title: Runtime paths
sections.explanation: Optional overrides for results, cache, memory log, and prompt template directories. Each comment states the default used by `default_config.py` when the variable is empty, and `TRADINGAGENTS_PROMPT_DIR` falls back to bundled templates for missing files.

sections.title: LLM provider and OpenAI settings
sections.explanation: `LLM_PROVIDER` picks the provider. The OpenAI block explains a subtle split: `OPENAI_USE_LOCAL` plus `OPENAI_BASE_URL` reroute core LLM and embedding calls to a local server, but OpenAI web-search tools still need a real `OPENAI_API_KEY` because local endpoints usually lack Responses web search.

sections.title: Other LLM providers and Azure
sections.explanation: One key per provider (Google, Anthropic, xAI, MiniMax, DeepSeek, DashScope for Qwen, Zhipu for GLM, OpenRouter) plus the four Azure OpenAI settings. Ollama needs no key; its URL is configured through the backend URL instead.

sections.title: Trading and data APIs
sections.explanation: Alpaca key, secret, and `ALPACA_USE_PAPER=True`, followed by Finnhub, FRED, FXMacroData (with a keyless `FXMACRODATA_ENABLED` USD-only mode), CoinDesk, and an optional Alpha Vantage fallback.

tradingagents/dataflows/config.py.overview: The runtime configuration and API key resolver used throughout the data and LLM layers. It loads `.env` at import, keeps a module-level copy of `DEFAULT_CONFIG` that callers can update with `set_config`, and exposes one getter per credential with a fixed precedence: keys set at runtime from the WebUI, then environment variables, then config values. It is the second half of the Central Configuration tour step.

sections.title: Module state and dotenv
sections.explanation: Calls `load_dotenv()` at import so environment variables from `.env` are available to every getter. Three module globals hold state: the active config dict, a derived `DATA_DIR`, and `_runtime_api_keys`, a dictionary the WebUI fills so keys entered in the browser override `.env` values.

sections.title: Config accessors
sections.explanation: `initialize_config` lazily copies `DEFAULT_CONFIG`; `set_config` merges overrides with `dict.update` (a shallow merge, so nested dicts like `deep_llm_params` are replaced, not merged). `get_config` returns a copy so callers cannot mutate the shared config by accident.

sections.title: Runtime key store
sections.explanation: Setter, getter, and clear functions for the WebUI-provided keys. `set_runtime_api_keys` updates rather than replaces, so partial updates keep earlier keys; `get_runtime_api_keys` again returns a copy.

sections.title: Key resolution precedence
sections.explanation: `get_api_key` implements the three-tier lookup: non-empty runtime key, then `os.getenv`, then the config entry. Note that an empty runtime string is skipped, but an empty environment variable is returned as-is because only `None` falls through to config. `_coerce_bool` normalizes strings like `"true"`, `"1"`, `"on"` for boolean flags.

sections.title: OpenAI and local endpoint helpers
sections.explanation: Helpers decide whether to route to a local OpenAI-compatible server. Environment values take priority over config for `OPENAI_USE_LOCAL`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL`, and the embedding model (defaulting to `text-embedding-ada-002`). `get_openai_client_config` builds SDK kwargs and substitutes the placeholder key `local-llm` in local mode, since many local servers ignore but still require an API key; the docstring explains why web-search tools are excluded from local routing.

sections.title: Per-provider key getters
sections.explanation: Thin wrappers around `get_api_key` for each provider, plus `get_llm_api_key`, which maps a provider name (for example `qwen` to the DashScope key and `glm` to the Zhipu key) to its getter. Unknown providers such as Ollama return an empty string rather than raising.

sections.title: Data and broker key getters
sections.explanation: Getters for Finnhub, Alpaca, FRED, CoinDesk, and FXMacroData keys. `get_alpaca_use_paper` stringifies booleans because the WebUI may send real bools while `.env` provides strings. `is_fxmacrodata_enabled` turns the integration on whenever a key exists, otherwise honors the explicit enable flag. The module ends by calling `initialize_config()` so config is ready at import.

tradingagents/default_config.py.overview: The single source of truth for default settings, exported as the `DEFAULT_CONFIG` dictionary. It covers storage paths, memory behavior, LLM selection and per-model reasoning params, debate depth, trading mode, deterministic risk sizing, the safety layer, alerts, portfolio and regime intelligence, concurrency delays, prompt context budgets, data tool timeouts, and API key placeholders. The WebUI, CLI, and Python users copy it and override keys per run, as described in the Central Configuration tour step.

sections.title: Paths and memory settings
sections.explanation: Paths default under `~/.tradingagents` or the package directory, but each can be overridden through environment variables read at import time (`TRADINGAGENTS_RESULTS_DIR`, `TRADINGAGENTS_MEMORY_LOG_PATH`, `TRADINGAGENTS_AGENT_MEMORY_DIR`, `TRADINGAGENTS_CACHE_DIR`). The memory block enables outcome reflections and FinMem-style maintenance (decay, near-duplicate pruning, per-collection caps). Because these `os.getenv` calls run at import, changing the environment later does not update the dict.

sections.title: LLM settings
sections.explanation: Selects the provider (from `LLM_PROVIDER`) and the two model tiers: a deep thinker for judges and a cheaper quick thinker for most agents. Provider-specific knobs default to `None`, and `deep_llm_params`/`quick_llm_params` carry Responses API style reasoning effort, verbosity, and `store: False`.

sections.title: Debate depth and trading mode
sections.explanation: `max_debate_rounds` and `max_risk_discuss_rounds` feed `ConditionalLogic`; `max_recur_limit` becomes the LangGraph recursion limit in `Propagator`. `allow_shorts` switches between investment mode (BUY/HOLD/SELL) and trading mode (LONG/NEUTRAL/SHORT). Risk sizing and protective bracket orders are on by default.

sections.title: Safety and alerts
sections.explanation: Deterministic guardrails independent of agent reasoning: per-order notional cap, symbol concentration limit, daily-loss and drawdown circuit breakers, a consecutive-rejection halt, and an optional daily token budget. Alert channels (Telegram, webhook) are only active once their credentials are set, with a cooldown to suppress duplicates.

sections.title: Portfolio and regime intelligence
sections.explanation: Parameters for correlation- and volatility-aware sizing of new long exposure, and for fit-free market regime detection. Each penalty has a floor (`portfolio_min_size_factor`, `regime_min_risk_multiplier`) so combined multipliers never shrink a trade to nothing silently.

sections.title: Execution and context budgets
sections.explanation: Delays between analyst starts and tool calls reduce provider rate-limit hits when analysts run in parallel. The `report_context_*` and `debate_digest_*` keys bound how much analyst evidence and debate history is injected into downstream prompts, and `include_full_reports_in_prompts` defaults off because full reports are slow. The last two keys cap tool-call loops per analyst.

sections.title: Data tool settings
sections.explanation: Timeouts, output token caps, and search breadth for news, fundamentals, macro, and Google News tools. Semantic retry re-runs low-quality web-search output once, except for the listed global/macro tools. `data_fallback_enabled` gates the yfinance backup.

sections.title: API key placeholders
sections.explanation: Keys default to `None` so `dataflows/config.get_api_key` can fall back to them only when no runtime or environment value exists. `alpaca_use_paper` is the string `"True"`, matching how environment values arrive. FXMacroData lists default currencies and FX pairs.

cli/main.py.overview: The Typer-based terminal interface (`python -m cli.main`). It collects selections interactively, builds a config from `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, constructs `TradingAgentsGraph`, then streams graph state chunks into a Rich live dashboard showing agent progress, messages, tool calls, and the current report. After the stream it extracts the final action, writes the audit log and decision memory, clears checkpoints, and prints a full team-by-team report. It is the main file of the CLI Entry Point tour step.

sections.title: Imports and Typer app
sections.explanation: Imports Rich layout widgets, the graph, checkpoint cleanup, the run audit logger, and `trade_intent_action`. `from cli.utils import *` brings in all prompt helpers. A single Typer app is created with shell completion enabled.

sections.title: MessageBuffer state
sections.explanation: `MessageBuffer` is the UI model: bounded deques of messages and tool calls, a status per agent (including a Portfolio Manager label used for the risk judge), and report sections keyed by the same names as `AgentState` fields. `_update_current_report` shows the last non-empty section in dict order (not strictly the most recently updated), and `_update_final_report` assembles the full markdown grouped by team. A single module-level instance is shared by all functions.

sections.title: Live layout rendering
sections.explanation: `create_layout` splits the screen into header, progress, messages, analysis, and footer regions. `update_display` rebuilds each panel from `message_buffer`: a team-grouped status table with spinners for in-progress agents, the latest 12 messages and tool calls (truncated for width), the current report as Markdown, and a footer of tool/LLM/report counts.

sections.title: Interactive selections
sections.explanation: `get_user_selections` prints a welcome banner and walks through numbered steps: ticker, analysts, research depth, provider, optional backend URL for providers that need one, quick and deep models, provider-specific Gemini/Claude options, checkpoint resume, and output language. The analysis date is always today. Gotcha: `get_ticker` is redefined at the bottom of this section, shadowing the validating version imported from `cli.utils`, so the CLI actually uses `typer.prompt` with a default of `SPY`.

sections.title: Final report display
sections.explanation: `display_complete_report` prints nested Rich panels for the analyst reports, research debate, trader plan, risk debate, and portfolio manager decision from the final state. `update_research_team_status` bulk-updates the researchers and trader.

sections.title: Run setup and config
sections.explanation: `run_analysis` maps the depth choice (1/3/5) onto both debate round limits and a named `research_depth`, copies provider and model selections into a fresh config, and forces investment mode. It then uses graph internals directly: `propagator.create_initial_state`, `_resolve_memory_log_outcomes`, `_graph_args_for_run`, and `_graph_for_run` (which may return a checkpointer context), and starts the run audit log with an initial snapshot.

sections.title: Streaming chunk handling
sections.explanation: Iterates `compiled_graph.stream(...)` in `values` mode, so each chunk is the full state. It logs the last message and any tool calls, then infers progress from which state fields are populated: analyst reports complete analysts in sequence, debate histories update researchers, and risk responses update the risk team. The inner `finally` always exits the checkpointer context, even on failure.

sections.title: Finalization and error handling
sections.explanation: The final action prefers the typed `final_trade_intent` and falls back to `process_signal` on the free-text decision. On success it logs state, finishes the audit run, stores the decision in the memory log, and clears the checkpoint if enabled. On any exception it marks the run failed with the last trace chunk before re-raising, then the UI marks everything complete and prints the report.

sections.title: CLI command entry
sections.explanation: The `analyze` Typer command simply calls `run_analysis`, and the module runs the app when executed directly.

cli/models.py.overview: Defines the `AnalystType` enum used by the CLI to identify the five analyst roles. Its string values (`market`, `social`, `news`, `fundamentals`, `macro`) are passed to `TradingAgentsGraph` as the selected analysts, as seen in the CLI Entry Point tour step.

sections.title: AnalystType enum
sections.explanation: Subclassing both `str` and `Enum` makes members compare equal to plain strings, which is why `cli/main.py` can test `"social" in selections["analysts"]` and pass `analyst.value` to the graph. The `List`, `Optional`, `Dict`, and `BaseModel` imports are unused leftovers.

cli/utils.py.overview: Interactive prompt helpers for the CLI built on `questionary`. Each function asks one question (ticker, date, analysts, depth, provider, models, provider-specific options, checkpointing, language) with validation and styling, and exits the process if the user cancels. Model and provider choices come from `tradingagents.openai_model_registry`, so the CLI shares the WebUI's catalog. It supports the CLI Entry Point tour step.

sections.title: Imports and analyst order
sections.explanation: Imports `questionary`, the provider/model registry, and `AnalystType`. `ANALYST_ORDER` pairs display names with enum values to define the checkbox order. Note that `console` here is the `rich.console` module, not a `Console` instance, so the `console.print(...)` calls in this file would fail with an AttributeError on the cancel paths.

sections.title: Ticker and date prompts
sections.explanation: `get_ticker` validates non-empty input and upper-cases it; `get_analysis_date` checks both a `YYYY-MM-DD` regex and a real `strptime` parse. The CLI's `main.py` overrides `get_ticker` with its own version and always uses today's date, so these are effectively unused there.

sections.title: Analyst and depth selection
sections.explanation: A checkbox requires at least one analyst. Research depth maps Shallow/Medium/Deep to 1/3/5 rounds, which `run_analysis` uses for both debate round limits.

sections.title: Provider and runtime options
sections.explanation: Provider choices come from `get_llm_provider_options()`. Small helpers ask whether to enable checkpoint resume, the output language (default English), a Gemini thinking level, a Claude effort level, and an optional backend URL; an empty string means provider default.

sections.title: Model selection with custom IDs
sections.explanation: Quick and deep model menus are built from `get_model_options_for_provider(provider, mode)`. Choosing the `custom` option falls through to `_prompt_custom_model_id`, which asks for a free-form model ID (or a deployment name for Azure), so newly released models work before the catalog is updated.

tradingagents/agents/utils/agent_states..overview: Declares the typed state shared by every node in the LangGraph workflow. `AgentState` extends LangGraph's `MessagesState` with the ticker, date, per-analyst reports, the structured report context, nested debate states for the research and risk teams, and the final decision fields including the typed trade intent. It is the data contract at the heart of the Graph Orchestration Core tour step.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports `TypedDict`, `Annotated`, and LangGraph primitives. Several imports (`ChatOpenAI`, `ToolNode`, `StateGraph`, the wildcard agents import) are not used by the state definitions themselves.

sections.title: Research debate state
sections.explanation: `InvestDebateState` holds both concatenated histories (`bull_history`, `bear_history`, `history`) and per-message lists used for chat-style display in the UI. `count` tracks the number of turns, and `current_response` is checked by `ConditionalLogic` to decide who speaks next.

sections.title: Risk debate state
sections.explanation: `RiskDebateState` mirrors the research version for three speakers (risky, safe, neutral), with `latest_speaker` driving the round-robin in `should_continue_risk_analysis` and `judge_decision` holding the risk manager's ruling.

sections.title: AgentState
sections.explanation: The top-level graph state. Fields are grouped by pipeline stage: identity (`company_of_interest`, `trade_date`, `sender`), five analyst reports plus `report_context`, the investment debate and plan, the trader plan, the risk debate, and the final outputs. `final_trade_intent` stores the typed JSON intent while `recommended_action` holds the executable signal; the `Annotated` strings serve as documentation rather than reducers.

tradingagents/graph/conditional_logic.py.overview: Routing functions used as LangGraph conditional edges. Analyst routers loop an analyst through its tool node while the last message contains tool calls, and debate routers alternate speakers until a round limit derived from config is reached. It is part of the Graph Orchestration Core tour step.

sections.title: Round limits
sections.explanation: Stores `max_debate_rounds` and `max_risk_discuss_rounds`, which come from config (and from the CLI depth choice).

sections.title: Analyst tool loops
sections.explanation: Five nearly identical routers return the analyst's tool node name (for example `tools_market`) if the last message requested tools, otherwise the matching `Msg Clear ...` node that cleans up messages before moving on. The returned strings must match node names registered in the graph setup.

sections.title: Research debate routing
sections.explanation: Stops after `2 * max_debate_rounds` turns (one bull and one bear per round) and hands off to the Research Manager. Otherwise it alternates by checking whether the current response starts with `Bull`, so the bull and bear nodes must prefix their responses accordingly.

sections.title: Risk debate routing
sections.explanation: Ends after `3 * max_risk_discuss_rounds` turns and routes to the Risk Judge. Otherwise it rotates Risky, then Safe, then Neutral, based on `latest_speaker`. It defensively initializes `latest_speaker` if missing, though `Propagator` already seeds it with `Risky`.

tradingagents/graph/propagation.py.overview: `Propagator` builds the initial `AgentState` for a run and the arguments passed to the compiled graph's invoke/stream call. It guarantees every field the nodes read exists with an empty default and sets the LangGraph recursion limit. It is part of the Graph Orchestration Core tour step and is called directly by the CLI.

sections.title: Imports and constructor
sections.explanation: Imports the state types and stores `max_recur_limit` (200 by default, from config).

sections.title: Initial state
sections.explanation: Seeds `messages` with the ticker as a human message, keeps the original ticker format so crypto symbols like `BTC/USD` survive, and initializes both debate states with zero counts and empty histories. The risk debate starts with `latest_speaker` set to `Risky`, and `current_position` defaults to `NEUTRAL`. Empty strings and dicts for all reports avoid key errors in downstream nodes.

sections.title: Graph invocation args
sections.explanation: Returns `stream_mode: values`, so each streamed chunk is the full state (which `cli/main.py` relies on), plus the recursion limit config.

tradingagents/graph/setup.py.overview: Builds the LangGraph `StateGraph` that defines the whole multi-agent pipeline. `GraphSetup` receives the two LLMs, the toolkit, tool nodes, per-agent memories and the conditional-routing logic from `TradingAgentsGraph`, creates every agent node, wraps each one with run-audit logging, and wires the edges: analysts (in parallel or in sequence), the shared report-context builder, the bull/bear debate, the research manager, the trader, and the risk debate ending at the Risk Judge. This is the core of tour step 4 (graph orchestration).

sections.title: Imports and dependencies
sections.explanation: Pulls in LangGraph primitives (`StateGraph`, `START`, `END`, `ToolNode`), the wildcard agent factory exports from `tradingagents.agents`, the shared `AgentState` schema, the report-context node factory and the run audit logger. `ConditionalLogic` is a sibling module that supplies the routing functions used on conditional edges.

sections.title: GraphSetup constructor
sections.explanation: Stores every collaborator the graph needs: a quick-thinking LLM for analysts and debaters, a deep-thinking LLM for managers and the trader, the toolkit, pre-built tool nodes, five memory stores and the config dict. The class has no logic of its own at construction time; all wiring happens later in `setup_graph`.

sections.title: Run-audit node wrapper
sections.explanation: `_wrap_node_with_run_logging` decorates a node function so each invocation emits a `node_execution` or `node_error` event with elapsed time, then re-raises errors unchanged. After success it scans the returned partial state for known output keys (reports, plans, final decision and intent), report-context stats and evidence scoreboard, and the latest debate responses, and logs each as an agent output. Because it inspects only the returned dict, it works uniformly for every agent without the agents knowing about auditing.

sections.title: Parallel analyst worker
sections.explanation: `_create_parallel_analysts_coordinator` returns a single graph node that runs all selected analysts itself. Each worker deep-copies the state, sleeps a configurable `analyst_call_delay`, runs the analyst, executes one round of tool calls via the analyst's `ToolNode` if requested, re-runs the analyst, and clears messages with the matching delete node (only when all messages have IDs). It also pushes status and partial reports to the optional Web UI `app_state`, which is imported lazily so the graph still works without the UI. Note the `social` analyst writes to `sentiment_report`, not `social_report`.

sections.title: Fan-out and report merge
sections.explanation: Submits analysts to a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with staggered starts (`analyst_start_delay`) to soften API rate limits, then collects results with `as_completed`; a failed analyst falls back to the original state. The merge step starts from a deep copy of the input state and copies only each analyst's report field, taken from the last message content or the report key. Missing reports are set to an empty string so downstream nodes never hit a `KeyError`.

sections.title: Parallel first risk round
sections.explanation: Runs the Risky, Safe and Neutral debaters concurrently for the first round only, each on its own deep-copied state. The results are merged into one `risk_debate_state` by appending each speaker's response to its own history, message list and the combined history, then advancing `count` by the number of responses actually produced. Later rounds stay sequential through conditional edges, so this saves latency without changing the debate's round-counting logic.

sections.title: Creating agent nodes
sections.explanation: `setup_graph` refuses an empty analyst list, reads `parallel_analysts`, and builds analyst nodes plus their message-delete and tool nodes for each selected analyst type. Researchers and debaters use the quick LLM, while the research manager, trader and risk manager use the deep LLM and receive the config. Every node is wrapped with run logging before it is registered.

sections.title: Analyst wiring: parallel vs sequential
sections.explanation: Creates the `StateGraph(AgentState)` and adds the `Build Report Context` node. In parallel mode the graph is simply START -> Parallel Analysts -> Build Report Context -> Bull Researcher. In sequential mode each analyst gets its own node, tool node and `Msg Clear` node, with conditional edges from `should_continue_<type>` looping through tools until the analyst is done, then chaining to the next analyst and finally to the report-context builder.

sections.title: Debate and risk edges
sections.explanation: Registers the nodes shared by both modes and the conditional edges for the bull/bear debate (looping until `should_continue_debate` routes to the Research Manager), then Research Manager -> Trader. The trader either feeds the parallel first risk round or goes straight to the Risky Analyst; the risk debaters rotate Risky -> Safe -> Neutral via `should_continue_risk_analysis` until the Risk Judge ends the graph. The uncompiled workflow is returned so the caller can compile it with or without a checkpointer.

tradingagents/graph/trading_graph.py.overview: `TradingAgentsGraph` is the main facade for the framework: it turns a config dict into LLM clients, memories, tool nodes and a compiled LangGraph, then runs it for one ticker and date via `propagate`. Around the run it handles optional checkpointing, run-audit logging, persisting full states to JSON, storing decisions in a memory log, and resolving earlier decisions' outcomes into reflections. It is the entry point the CLI and Web UI call, and the centerpiece of tour step 4.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Brings in yfinance (used only for outcome returns), the LLM client factory, the agents package, memory classes, the trade-intent helper, state types, the model-parameter registry, config accessors and ticker utilities. The graph helper modules (checkpointer, conditional logic, setup, propagation, reflection, signal processing) are imported relatively from the same package.

sections.title: Constructor: LLM configuration
sections.explanation: Pushes the config into the dataflows layer with `set_config`, creates cache and results directories, and normalizes per-role model params through `normalize_model_params` so only knobs valid for each model are passed. An integer `research_depth` is mapped back to a label purely for logging. If the provider is `openai` but a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint is enabled, it is switched to `local_openai`; provider-specific effort kwargs and callbacks are added before `create_llm_client` builds the deep and quick clients.

sections.title: Constructor: memories, tools, graph
sections.explanation: Creates the `Toolkit`, five `FinancialSituationMemory` stores and a `TradingMemoryLog`, then the tool nodes, `ConditionalLogic` (debate round limits), `GraphSetup`, `Propagator`, `Reflector` and `SignalProcessor`. The workflow is built once and compiled once without a checkpointer; the uncompiled `workflow` is kept so a checkpointed variant can be compiled per run.

sections.title: Provider kwargs and per-run graph
sections.explanation: `_get_provider_kwargs` maps provider-specific config keys (Google thinking level, OpenAI/xAI reasoning effort, Anthropic effort) to client kwargs. When `checkpoint_enabled` is set, `_graph_for_run` enters a checkpointer context manually and compiles a fresh graph with it, and `_graph_args_for_run` adds a `thread_id` derived from ticker and date so an interrupted run can resume.

sections.title: Forward return helpers
sections.explanation: Converts tickers to Yahoo format, picks a benchmark (SPY for stocks, BTC-USD for crypto, none when the ticker is the benchmark), and computes the next-open to N-bar-later open return with yfinance. Every failure path returns `None` rather than raising, and returns are only computed when enough bars exist before the cutoff date, which avoids look-ahead.

sections.title: Resolving pending decision outcomes
sections.explanation: Before each run, earlier logged decisions for the ticker that are older than the current trade date are scored: raw return, benchmark return and alpha are computed, the reflector writes a reflection, and the memory log entry is updated. The prompt explicitly states the return is the underlying asset's hypothetical return before costs, not account PnL, so the reflection does not over-attribute results.

sections.title: Per-agent outcome reflection
sections.explanation: Reloads the original run's final state snapshot from the run log so each agent reflects on what it actually saw, then calls `reflect_on_outcome` across all five memories and optionally runs memory maintenance. The whole block is wrapped in a broad `try/except`, matching the docstring's promise that reflection must never break the current analysis.

sections.title: Tool node definitions
sections.explanation: Groups toolkit methods into one `ToolNode` per analyst type: market (Alpaca and stockstats), social (OpenAI stock news and Reddit), news (Google, Finnhub, CoinDesk, plus optional OpenAI global news), fundamentals (OpenAI, DeFi Llama, Finnhub insider data, SimFin) and macro (FRED-style macro, yield curve, FX data). These nodes are used by the graph's tool-calling loops.

sections.title: propagate: running the graph
sections.explanation: Resolves old outcomes, builds the initial state, starts a run in the audit logger and snapshots the initial state. In debug mode it streams chunks and pretty-prints messages; otherwise it calls `invoke`. Failures finish the run as `failed` and re-raise, and the checkpointer context is always exited. On success the signal comes from the structured `final_trade_intent` when available, falling back to LLM signal extraction; Web UI runtime context is logged best-effort, the decision is stored in the memory log, and the checkpoint is cleared.

sections.title: State log, reflection, signal
sections.explanation: `_log_state` copies the key reports, debate histories, plans and final decision into a per-date dict and writes it to `results_dir/<ticker>/TradingAgentsStrategy_logs/full_states_log.json`, using `safe_ticker_component` to keep ticker names path-safe. `reflect_and_remember` lets callers manually feed returns back into each role's memory, and `process_signal` delegates to `SignalProcessor`.

tradingagents/llm_clients/base_client.py.overview: Defines the small abstract contract every LLM provider client implements, plus a helper that flattens provider responses into plain text. The factory in `factory.py` returns subclasses of `BaseLLMClient`, and `TradingAgentsGraph` only relies on `get_llm()`, which keeps provider differences out of the graph code (tour step 5).

sections.title: Response content normalization
sections.explanation: `normalize_content` handles providers that return message content as a list of typed blocks (for example text blocks mixed with reasoning or tool blocks). It keeps only text items and joins them with newlines, mutating the response in place, so agents can always treat `response.content` as a string.

sections.title: BaseLLMClient core
sections.explanation: Stores the model name, optional base URL and arbitrary kwargs. `get_provider_name` prefers an explicit `provider` attribute and otherwise derives a name from the class name, and `warn_if_unknown_model` emits a `RuntimeWarning` rather than failing when a model is not in the known list, so new model IDs still work.

sections.title: Abstract interface
sections.explanation: Subclasses must implement `get_llm()`, which returns a LangChain-compatible chat model, and `validate_model()`, which reports whether the model is recognized for that provider.

tradingagents/llm_clients/factory.py.overview: The single entry point for building an LLM client from a provider name. It routes OpenAI and every OpenAI-compatible provider to `OpenAIClient`, and Google, Anthropic and Azure to their own clients. `TradingAgentsGraph` calls `create_llm_client` twice, once for the quick and once for the deep model (tour step 5).

sections.title: OpenAI-compatible providers
sections.explanation: `_OPENAI_COMPATIBLE` lists providers that speak the OpenAI chat API (local endpoints, xAI, MiniMax, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, Ollama, OpenRouter). Keeping them in one tuple means adding such a provider mostly requires an entry here and a base URL in `openai_client.py`.

sections.title: create_llm_client dispatch
sections.explanation: Lowercases the provider (defaulting to `openai`) and returns the matching client. Imports are done lazily inside each branch so optional SDKs such as Google or Anthropic integrations are only needed when that provider is actually selected. Unknown providers raise `ValueError`.

tradingagents/llm_clients/openai_client..overview: Implements the client for OpenAI and all OpenAI-compatible providers. Native OpenAI and local endpoints are delegated to the project's `gpt5_llm.get_chat_model` (which handles Responses API models), while other providers get a `ChatOpenAI` subclass pointed at their base URL. A DeepSeek-specific subclass preserves `reasoning_content` across turns (tour step 5).

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Uses LangChain's `ChatOpenAI` and `AIMessage`, the shared `normalize_content` helper and a provider model validator.

sections.title: NormalizedChatOpenAI
sections.explanation: Overrides `invoke` so every response passes through `normalize_content`, and defaults `with_structured_output` to the `function_calling` method, which is more widely supported by compatible providers than JSON-schema mode. `_input_to_messages` converts a prompt value or list into a message list for the DeepSeek override.

sections.title: DeepSeek reasoning passthrough
sections.explanation: DeepSeek returns `reasoning_content` that must be sent back on later assistant turns. The subclass copies it from `AIMessage.additional_kwargs` into the outgoing payload and captures it from responses into `additional_kwargs`. It also blocks structured output for `deepseek-reasoner`, which does not support it.

sections.title: Provider endpoints and key variables
sections.explanation: Maps each compatible provider to its default base URL and the environment variable that holds its API key. Ollama has no key variable because it runs locally.

sections.title: OpenAIClient.get_llm
sections.explanation: For `openai` and `local_openai` it requires an API key (a placeholder `local-llm` key is allowed for local endpoints) and delegates to `get_chat_model`, passing the model role and remaining kwargs. For other providers it builds kwargs from the provider table, raises a clear error when the required key is missing, forwards only a safe allowlist of options (timeouts, retries, reasoning effort, callbacks, HTTP clients), and picks the DeepSeek subclass when needed.

sections.title: Model validation
sections.explanation: OpenAI and local models always validate, because the registry handles arbitrary and future model IDs; other providers are checked against their known model list.

tradingagents/openai_model_registry.py.overview: Central registry of OpenAI model capabilities and the helpers that turn user-chosen settings into valid request parameters. The Web UI uses it to build model and provider dropdowns and to show only the controls a model supports; the runtime uses `normalize_model_params`, `describe_model_params` and `apply_responses_model_params` so reasoning models get effort/verbosity settings and chat models get temperature/top_p. It complements the LLM provider layer in tour step 5.

sections.title: Module header and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring states the purpose: one place that knows which knobs are valid per model family. It depends on `DEFAULT_CONFIG` for default model names and on the provider model catalog for non-OpenAI options.

sections.title: Option lists and parameter help
sections.explanation: Defines allowed values for reasoning summary and text verbosity, and `PARAMETER_HELP`, user-facing explanations of each knob's cost and quality trade-off that the UI can show as hints.

sections.title: Reasoning model spec builder
sections.explanation: `_reasoning_spec` produces a uniform capability dict for Responses API reasoning models: effort options, verbosity and summary support, no temperature/top_p, and per-role defaults (quick vs deep). Using a builder keeps the large registry below consistent.

sections.title: MODEL_REGISTRY entries
sections.explanation: Lists the known models with labels, descriptions, roles, visibility and role defaults. Some entries are hidden (`visible=False`) and kept only so old saved configs still resolve. `gpt-4.1` is a hand-written chat-API spec that supports temperature and top_p instead of reasoning controls, and it doubles as the fallback template for unknown models.

sections.title: Model spec lookup and options
sections.explanation: `get_model_spec` resolves an exact match, then a dated snapshot of a known alias by prefix, then any name matching the numbered `gpt-N` pattern as a forward-compatible reasoning model (adding `none` effort only for versions below 6), and finally falls back to a chat-model spec. `get_openai_model_options` builds Dash select options filtered by visibility and role.

sections.title: Provider options and UI metadata
sections.explanation: `LLM_PROVIDER_OPTIONS` lists every selectable provider and `PROVIDER_UI_METADATA` describes, per provider, the API key variable, endpoint text, whether the backend URL field is shown, whether custom model IDs are allowed, and summary pills for the UI.

sections.title: Provider and model choice helpers
sections.explanation: Small helpers used by the UI and runtime: provider metadata lookup with an OpenAI fallback, model options per provider (adding a `custom` entry where supported), default model per provider and role, resolving a `custom` selection to the typed model ID, and capability checks `is_responses_model` / `is_reasoning_model`. `get_default_model_params` falls back to the first role's defaults when a role is missing.

sections.title: Coercion and normalize_model_params
sections.explanation: Coercion helpers turn UI strings into bools, clamped floats and positive ints. `normalize_model_params` merges role defaults with user params and keeps only what the model spec supports, falling back to defaults on invalid values. It writes both canonical and alias keys (`text_verbosity` and `verbosity`, `reasoning_summary` and `summary`) so different downstream wrappers can read them.

sections.title: Applying params to Responses requests
sections.explanation: `apply_responses_model_params` maps normalized params onto a Responses API payload: verbosity goes under `text`, effort and summary under `reasoning` (summary is skipped when set to `none`), and sampling, output cap, store and parallel tool calls become top-level fields. The dataflows layer uses this for web-search tool calls.

sections.title: Describing params and UI control state
sections.explanation: `describe_model_params` renders a compact `effort=..., verbosity=...` string used in the startup log. `get_ui_control_state` returns the spec, defaults and description for Dash callbacks; for non-OpenAI providers it returns a spec with all OpenAI-specific controls disabled because those settings come from runtime config instead.

tradingagents/prompts/loader.py.overview: Loads model-facing prompts from Markdown templates so prompt wording lives outside the Python agent code. Templates are looked up first in an optional override directory set by `TRADINGAGENTS_PROMPT_DIR`, then in the bundled `templates/` folder, and rendered with Python `str.format_map`. This is the mechanism behind tour step 6 (external prompt templates).

sections.title: Constants and error type
sections.explanation: Defines the override environment variable name, the bundled template directory next to this file, and `PromptTemplateError`, a `ValueError` subclass used for every loading and rendering failure.

sections.title: Search roots and path safety
sections.explanation: `_template_roots` returns the override directory (if set) ahead of the bundled one, which gives per-file override with fallback. `_safe_template_path` adds a `.md` suffix and rejects empty names, NUL bytes, absolute paths and `..` segments; `_resolve_template_path` additionally checks the resolved path stays inside the root, guarding against symlink escapes.

sections.title: load_prompt and render_prompt
sections.explanation: `load_prompt` returns the first existing template across roots or raises a not-found error. `render_prompt` fills placeholders with `format_map` and converts a missing key into a `PromptTemplateError` naming the placeholder and template. Because Python formatting is used, literal braces in templates must be doubled.

sections.title: Listing templates
sections.explanation: `list_prompt_templates` collects relative `.md` paths from all existing roots into a sorted, de-duplicated list, useful for tooling or tests that check every expected template exists.

tradingagents/prompts/templates/README.m.overview: Documentation for the prompt template folder. It explains that agent behavior can be tuned by editing these Markdown files, lists the template groups, and documents the `TRADINGAGENTS_PROMPT_DIR` override with fallback that `loader.py` implements (tour step 6).

sections.title: Purpose and placeholders
sections.explanation: States that these files hold the model-facing prompts and that placeholders such as `{ticker}` and `{analysis_content}` are filled at runtime by the agent modules via `render_prompt`.

sections.title: Template groups
sections.explanation: Maps folders to pipeline roles: shared scaffolding, analysts, researchers, managers, trader, risk debaters, trading-mode instructions, and graph-level prompts for signal extraction and reflection.

sections.title: Local override directory
sections.explanation: Shows how to keep local prompt edits outside the repository with `TRADINGAGENTS_PROMPT_DIR`. The override folder only needs the files being changed, using the same group path; any missing template falls back to the bundled version.

tradingagents/prompts/templates/trader/t.overview: The trader agent's system prompt template. It is short on purpose: the role statement plus three placeholders that the trader module fills with trading-mode context, retrieved similar-situation reflections, and the persistent decision log. It is a concrete example of the external template approach in tour step 6.

sections.title: Role and trader context
sections.explanation: Sets the agent's role and injects `{trader_context}`, which carries runtime instructions such as the trading mode and current position supplied by the trader code.

sections.title: Memory placeholders
sections.explanation: `{past_memory_str}` receives reflections retrieved from the trader's situation memory, and `{decision_memory_str}` receives lessons from the persistent decision log for this symbol and recent cross-ticker setups. Together they close the learning loop described in tour step 12.

tradingagents/agents/analysts/market_ana.overview: Factory for the market (technical) analyst node. Depending on whether online tools and Alpaca credentials are available, it chooses a set of technical tools, renders its prompt from external templates, runs its own bounded tool-calling loop with de-duplication, forces a `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL`, normalizes the markdown, and appends a deterministic market-regime block. It is the worked example of an analyst in tour step 7.

sections.title: Imports and prompt capture fallback
sections.explanation: Imports LangChain prompt and message types and the template loader. `capture_agent_prompt` comes from the Web UI when available; otherwise a no-op stub is defined so the agent runs headless (CLI, tests) without the UI package.

sections.title: Report markdown normalization
sections.explanation: Uses regexes to turn inline labels like `a) Conclusion` or `Entry Conditions:` into `##` headings, put the final proposal on its own block, split table rows that were emitted on one line, and collapse excess blank lines. This makes LLM output render consistently in the UI and reports.

sections.title: Tool selection and workflow text
sections.explanation: Inside the node, crypto is detected from the ticker format and Alpaca availability is checked. With online tools and Alpaca it offers the technical brief, Alpaca data and online stockstats; without Alpaca it falls back to offline stockstats. The workflow instructions are then assembled to mention only tools that actually exist in this run, so the model is not told to call unavailable tools.

sections.title: Prompt assembly and capture
sections.explanation: Loads an intro template (with or without the technical brief), renders `analysts/market_system`, and wraps it in the shared `analyst_tool_system` prompt with partials for tool names, date, ticker and asset context. The fully formatted system prompt is captured for the UI, with fallbacks if formatting fails.

sections.title: Bounded tool-calling loop
sections.explanation: Binds tools to the LLM and loops while the response requests tool calls, up to `max_tool_iterations_per_agent`. Each call is parsed from either dict or object form, keyed by name plus sorted JSON args, served from a cache if already run, and skipped once `max_same_tool_call_repeats` is exceeded. Tool calls and results are appended as `AIMessage`/`ToolMessage` pairs, and if the limit is hit the result is replaced by a note that the loop was halted.

sections.title: Ensuring a final proposal
sections.explanation: If the analysis is empty a limitation message is substituted. When the text lacks `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL:`, a second tool-free LLM call renders the `market_final_recommendation` template and its output is appended, so downstream agents always find a parseable proposal.

sections.title: Deterministic regime injection
sections.explanation: Appends a regime block computed from price and volume history (no LLM) to `market_report`, so every downstream agent sees the same risk-posture facts. Failures are logged and skipped. The node returns the new message and the `market_report` field.

tradingagents/agents/utils/agent_utils.p.overview: Defines the `Toolkit`: the LangChain `@tool` functions analysts can call, each a thin wrapper over `dataflows.interface`. Every tool is decorated with `timing_wrapper`, which adds timeouts, output-quality scoring, a semantic retry for weak web-search results, UI tool-call tracking and run-audit logging. It also provides capability checks (API keys, SimFin files) and the message-clearing node used between analysts. This is the tool layer of tour step 7.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: LangChain messages, prompts and the `tool` decorator, date utilities, the dataflows `interface` module that does the real data work, default config, the run audit logger and API key helpers.

sections.title: Output quality constants
sections.explanation: Minimum expected output length for selected web-search tools, tools excluded from semantic retry by default, phrases that indicate the model asked a follow-up question instead of answering, and phrases that legitimately produce short outputs (for example 'no data available').

sections.title: Follow-up detection and quality scoring
sections.explanation: `_is_trailing_interactive_followup` checks the last 700 characters for follow-up phrases after normalizing curly quotes and dashes. `_strip_trailing_interactive_followup` removes such trailing lines and their bullet options, keeping the original if nothing would remain. `_score_output_quality` flags empty, interactive, error-prefixed or undersized outputs, computes a score, and recommends a retry only for suspect outputs that are not explicit errors.

sections.title: Semantic retry policy
sections.explanation: Retries only web-search tools, only when enabled and under the retry limit, and only when quality scoring recommends it. Tools can be excluded through config (string or list). Global news is not retried when its output already meets the minimum length, which avoids paying for a second expensive web search.

sections.title: timing_wrapper decorator
sections.explanation: Wraps each tool so it runs in a thread pool with a timeout (extended for web-search tools); the executor is deliberately not used as a context manager because `__exit__` would wait for a hung worker and defeat the timeout. On timeout it returns an error string and logs a `timeout` tool call. Successful outputs are scored and retried with backoff when the retry policy says so, then recorded in the Web UI tool log and the run audit log. Exceptions are classified (timeouts, rate limits and others), logged, tracked as failed calls, and re-raised.

sections.title: Message clearing node
sections.explanation: `create_msg_delete` returns a node that emits a `RemoveMessage` for every message in state, keeping message history from growing across analyst stages.

sections.title: Toolkit config and capability checks
sections.explanation: `Toolkit` stores configuration at class level, so `update_config` affects every instance and the decorated static tools can read it through `Toolkit._config`. The `has_*` helpers check for API keys or the FXMacroData flag without raising, and `has_simfin_data` requires a full set of balance, cash-flow and income CSV files for either annual or quarterly frequency.

sections.title: News, social, market and fundamentals tools
sections.explanation: Static `@tool` methods with `Annotated` argument descriptions that become the LLM-visible schema. Each delegates to an `interface` function: Reddit and Finnhub news, Alpaca price data, offline and online stockstats indicators, Finnhub insider data, SimFin statements, CoinDesk and Google news, OpenAI web-search tools and earnings data. The `timing_wrapper` argument labels each tool by analyst type, and `uses_web_search=True` turns on the timeout extension and semantic retry.

sections.title: Macro and crypto fundamentals tools
sections.explanation: Macro tools for the macro analyst: overall macro analysis, OpenAI macro news, economic indicators, yield curve, global indicators, economic release calendar and FX rates (the last three backed by FXMacroData), plus DeFi Llama fundamentals for crypto assets.

sections.title: Market tables and technical brief
sections.explanation: `get_alpaca_data_report` returns a lookback window of bars. `get_stock_data_table` cleans timestamps into plain dates with regexes and falls back to the raw output on any error. `get_indicators_table` builds a markdown table of many indicators per date with fixed formatting and a static guide to swing-trading signals. `get_technical_brief` returns pre-analyzed multi-timeframe JSON so the LLM receives deterministic conclusions instead of raw numbers.

tradingagents/dataflows/interface.py.overview: The data access facade used by every toolkit tool. It hides the individual data utilities (Finnhub, SimFin, Google News, Reddit, stockstats, Alpaca, CoinDesk, DeFi Llama, earnings, macro and FXMacroData) behind functions that return LLM-ready markdown strings, prefer local caches before live APIs, and degrade to readable error or fallback text instead of raising. It also owns the OpenAI web-search calls with their Responses API parameters and empty-output fallbacks (tour step 7).

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports the per-source utility modules (several via wildcard), config accessors, OpenAI helpers from `interface_utils` (timeouts, response text extraction, depth profiles) and the model registry helpers used to shape Responses API requests.

sections.title: Fallback builders for empty web search
sections.explanation: `_cap_headline_sections` limits fallback payloads to N `###` sections and a character cap. When OpenAI web search returns nothing, the global, stock-news and fundamentals fallbacks assemble substitute content from Google News, Finnhub news and Finnhub insider data, each prefixed with a 'Fallback used because...' line so analysts know the source changed.

sections.title: Responses API request helpers
sections.explanation: Decides when the Responses API is used for web search, derives quick-model params with default output cap and store flag, and builds a request with developer/system and user messages, a `web_search` tool and source inclusion. `_create_response_with_output_cap_fallback` retries once without `max_output_tokens` if the API rejects that parameter.

sections.title: Finnhub and SimFin data
sections.explanation: `get_finnhub_news` reads cached news first and falls back to the live Finnhub API only when the cache is empty and online tools are enabled, labeling the source in the header. The insider sentiment, insider transactions and SimFin balance sheet, cash flow and income statement functions follow the same pattern of returning formatted markdown from local data.

sections.title: Google News and Reddit
sections.explanation: Google News queries that look like stock tickers are expanded with `$TICKER` and the company name from Alpaca, results are capped by configurable page and item limits, and duplicates are removed by a normalized title and link key. Reddit functions return global and company-specific posts over a lookback window.

sections.title: Stockstats indicators and history
sections.explanation: Single-indicator and window lookups wrap stockstats and catch errors. The alias map lets the LLM use either `close_50_sma` or `sma_50` style names, groups expand `bbands` and `stochrsi_14`, and timeframe keys are normalized to 1h/4h/1d. `get_stockstats_indicator_history` computes missing columns when needed and returns a compact markdown table capped at `max_points` rows.

sections.title: OpenAI web-search tools
sections.explanation: Stock news/sentiment, global news and fundamentals each read their timeout, output cap and fast-profile flags from config, choose the search context and lookback from research depth, and call either the Responses API with web search or plain chat completions for older models. Trailing follow-up questions are stripped, and empty output or exceptions return the deterministic fallbacks above, so a failing provider still yields usable evidence.

sections.title: DeFi Llama and Alpaca price data
sections.explanation: DeFi Llama fundamentals strip USD/USDT suffixes before lookup. `get_alpaca_data_window` computes a start date from the lookback and intentionally omits an end date to avoid subscription limits on recent data, then appends the latest quote. `get_alpaca_data` adds summary stats such as daily change, volume versus average, daily range, spread and an after-hours move estimate.

sections.title: Technical brief
sections.explanation: Lazily imports the technical brief builder, computes the multi-timeframe brief, and serializes it as JSON. On failure it returns a JSON error object instead of raising, so the analyst's tool loop always receives a parseable result.

sections.title: Earnings, macro and FX wrappers
sections.explanation: Thin pass-through functions to the earnings, macro and FXMacroData utilities. Note that `get_macro_analysis` accepts `lookback_days` but only passes `curr_date` to the underlying summary.

tradingagents/agents/managers/research_m.overview: Factory for the Research Manager node, the judge of the bull/bear investment debate. It combines the evidence-scored claim matrix, a compact debate digest, vector memories and the decision log, then asks the LLM for a structured `ResearchPlan`. The result becomes `investment_plan`, which the Trader consumes next. This is the final step of tour step 8 and the bridge into step 9.

sections.title: Imports and optional prompt capture
sections.explanation: Brings in the report-context helpers, the `ResearchPlan` schema and its Markdown renderer, trading-mode utilities, the persistent `TradingMemoryLog`, and the structured-output helpers. As in other agents, `capture_agent_prompt` falls back to a no-op when the web UI is unavailable.

sections.title: Factory and context assembly
sections.explanation: `bind_structured` is called once at factory time so a provider without structured output support degrades to free text instead of failing. Inside the node, trading-mode context supplies the allowed actions and the exact final-line format. The evidence bundle is requested with an adjudication objective, and two memory sources are combined: similarity-based memories (`memory.get_memories`) and the per-ticker decision log, both bounded by `as_of_date`.

sections.title: Prompt rendering and structured call
sections.explanation: All inputs go into the external `managers/research_manager` template, including `output_language`. `invoke_structured_or_freetext` tries the structured LLM and renders the `ResearchPlan` to Markdown, retrying as free text on failure. If a recommendation can be extracted, `ensure_final_transaction_proposal` guarantees the exact `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL: **X**` line that downstream parsing relies on.

sections.title: Writing the judge decision
sections.explanation: The node rebuilds `investment_debate_state` with `judge_decision` and `current_response` set to the plan, copying bull and bear histories through. Keeping `count` unchanged means the judge does not count as a debate turn. The plan is also published as the top-level `investment_plan` key for the Trader.

tradingagents/agents/researchers/bear_re.overview: Factory for the bear researcher node in the investment debate. Each turn it pulls a role-weighted evidence bundle from the shared report context, recalls similar past situations from memory, renders the external `researchers/bear_researcher` prompt, and appends a `Bear Analyst:` argument to the debate state. It is the mirror image of the bull researcher; together they feed the Research Manager covered in tour step 8.

sections.title: Imports and prompt capture
sections.explanation: Pulls in the shared context helpers (`get_agent_context_bundle`, `build_debate_digest`) and the prompt renderer. The `capture_agent_prompt` import is optional: when the `webui` package is not importable, a no-op fallback is defined so the agent still runs from the CLI or tests.

sections.title: Gathering debate evidence
sections.explanation: `create_bear_researcher(llm, memory)` returns a closure that LangGraph calls as a node. The objective string handed to `get_agent_context_bundle` embeds the latest opposing argument (`current_response`), so chunk retrieval is biased toward evidence that counters the bull case. Note that no `config` is passed here, so the context bundle uses default budgets. The memory lookup passes `as_of_date` to avoid leaking memories from after the trade date.

sections.title: Prompt rendering and LLM call
sections.explanation: The prompt is rendered from an external template with the claim matrix, the debate digest, full history and recalled memories. The fully rendered prompt is captured under `bear_report` for the web UI before a plain `llm.invoke` call; unlike the managers, researchers do not use structured output.

sections.title: Updating the debate state
sections.explanation: The response is prefixed with `Bear Analyst:` and appended to both the shared `history` and the side-specific `bear_history`, plus the `bear_messages` list used for conversation display. The bull side's fields are copied through unchanged, `current_response` is set so the opponent can rebut it, and `count` is incremented, which the conditional logic uses to decide when the debate ends.

tradingagents/agents/researchers/bull_re.overview: Factory for the bull researcher node in the investment debate. Each turn it pulls a role-weighted evidence bundle from the shared report context, recalls similar past situations from memory, renders the external `researchers/bull_researcher` prompt, and appends a `Bull Analyst:` argument to the debate state. It is the mirror image of the bear researcher; together they feed the Research Manager covered in tour step 8.

sections.title: Imports and prompt capture
sections.explanation: Pulls in the shared context helpers (`get_agent_context_bundle`, `build_debate_digest`) and the prompt renderer. The `capture_agent_prompt` import is optional: when the `webui` package is not importable, a no-op fallback is defined so the agent still runs from the CLI or tests.

sections.title: Gathering debate evidence
sections.explanation: `create_bull_researcher(llm, memory)` returns a closure that LangGraph calls as a node. The objective string handed to `get_agent_context_bundle` embeds the latest opposing argument (`current_response`), so chunk retrieval is biased toward evidence that counters the bear case. Note that no `config` is passed here, so the context bundle uses default budgets. The memory lookup passes `as_of_date` to avoid leaking memories from after the trade date.

sections.title: Prompt rendering and LLM call
sections.explanation: The prompt is rendered from an external template with the claim matrix, the debate digest, full history and recalled memories. The fully rendered prompt is captured under `bull_report` for the web UI before a plain `llm.invoke` call; unlike the managers, researchers do not use structured output.

sections.title: Updating the debate state
sections.explanation: The response is prefixed with `Bull Analyst:` and appended to both the shared `history` and the side-specific `bull_history`, plus the `bull_messages` list used for conversation display. The bear side's fields are copied through unchanged, `current_response` is set so the opponent can rebut it, and `count` is incremented, which the conditional logic uses to decide when the debate ends.

tradingagents/agents/utils/report_contex.overview: The shared evidence layer for every debate and decision agent. It splits the five analyst reports into sections and overlapping chunks, extracts coverage points, turns them into scored claims (freshness, numeric support, source quality, actionability, contradiction), builds a bullish/bearish evidence scoreboard, and retrieves role-weighted chunks under a token budget. Agents call `get_agent_context_bundle` to get pre-rendered prompt blocks instead of pasting full reports. This is the core of tour step 8.

sections.title: Report specs and context budgets
sections.explanation: `REPORT_SPECS` fixes the five analyst report keys and their display order. `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_CONFIG` holds every tunable budget (token budget, chunk size and overlap, point and claim lengths, digest limits); any key can be overridden through the main config. `SOURCE_PROFILE` assigns each report a source type and a static quality prior, with sentiment rated lowest and fundamentals highest.

sections.title: Signal lexicons and role weights
sections.explanation: Keyword tuples (`BULLISH_TERMS`, `BEARISH_TERMS`, `ACTIONABILITY_TERMS`) drive a simple lexical classifier rather than an LLM call, keeping context building deterministic and cheap. `ROLE_WEIGHTS` biases retrieval per agent, for example the safe debator weights macro highest while the trader weights the market report. The `ROLE_WEIGHTS.update` block aliases the path-style role names (`researchers/bull_researcher`) that agents actually pass. `STOPWORDS` filters generic terms from query matching.

sections.title: Text and score helpers
sections.explanation: `_get_context_config` merges user config over defaults. `_estimate_tokens` uses a rough four-characters-per-token heuristic. `truncate_for_prompt` is kept as a backward-compatible alias but now ignores `max_chars` and only normalizes. `_classify_signal` counts bullish versus bearish term hits and returns Mixed on ties, and the clamp/round helpers keep scores in [0, 1].

sections.title: Claim feature scoring
sections.explanation: These helpers score a single claim. Freshness parses ISO and US dates and decays with age relative to the trade date, ignoring dates after it; words like "latest" earn an implicit-recent score. Numeric support rewards figures, percentages and finance keywords; actionability rewards trading terms and favors technical sources; `_infer_horizon` labels claims as swing, event, macro or position. `_claim_terms` removes generic words so contradiction detection keys on material terms.

sections.title: Claim construction and contradictions
sections.explanation: `_initial_claim_scores` blends priority, numeric support, source quality, actionability and freshness into an evidence-strength score. `_build_claim_from_point` assigns a stable `claim_id`, direction, horizon and up to two evidence chunk references. `_apply_contradiction_scores` compares every opposing bullish/bearish pair; shared material terms raise a contradiction score (higher when from the same source type), which then discounts the composite in `_finalize_claim_score`. Pairs at or above 0.32 are reported as major contradictions.

sections.title: Evidence scoreboard
sections.explanation: `_side_score` averages the top five claims per direction, rewards source diversity and penalizes contradiction. `_build_evidence_scoreboard` declares a net direction only when one side leads by at least 0.08, assigns a high/medium/low confidence label, groups scores by source, and writes plain-language `manager_guidance` (mixed evidence favors HOLD/NEUTRAL). `_build_evidence_layer` runs this pipeline and stores claims, scoreboard and counts back into the context.

sections.title: Rendering the claim matrix
sections.explanation: These functions turn the structured scoreboard into prompt text. Each claim line shows its id, direction and key scores so the LLM can cite evidence by id. `_render_decision_claim_matrix` lists the top claims per report with a dominant direction, and falls back to lexical voting over raw coverage points when a report produced no claims.

sections.title: Section parsing and chunking
sections.explanation: Reports are split on Markdown headings, and candidate lines (at least 20 characters, not table separators, bullets stripped) are ranked by `_line_priority`, which favors digits, currency, percentages and trading keywords. `_chunk_text` cuts sections into overlapping chunks, preferring to break on newlines or spaces past 60 percent of the chunk length. `_score_chunk` combines role weight, query-term overlap and small bonuses for action words and numbers.

sections.title: Index building and retrieval
sections.explanation: `build_report_context_index` produces the versioned context index: per-report coverage points, summaries and chunk ids, a global overview, token statistics, and finally the evidence layer. `_select_chunks_for_agent` runs two passes under the token budget: a coverage pass that guarantees each report at least `min_chunks_per_report`, then a relevance pass that fills the remainder by score up to `max_chunks`.

sections.title: Prompt blocks and public entry points
sections.explanation: Renderers produce the full and compact analysis packets, a truncated memory-query context, and `all_reports_text`, which by default is a placeholder because full reports are only included when `include_full_reports_in_prompts` is set (a latency trade-off). `build_debate_digest` summarizes either the investment or risk debate with per-side message limits. `ensure_report_context` caches the index in state on purpose so each node does not rebuild it, and `get_agent_context_bundle` is the single API agents call. `create_report_context_node` exposes index building as a graph node.

tradingagents/agents/schemas.py.overview: Pydantic schemas for the decision agents' structured output and for the machine-readable `TradeIntent` that the execution layer consumes. It also holds Markdown renderers that always end with the canonical `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL` line, and the deterministic mapping from a risk decision to position transitions and broker actions. Central to tour step 9 and the hand-off into safe execution.

sections.title: Protective price extraction
sections.explanation: The module docstring states the key rule: only BUY/HOLD/SELL or LONG/NEUTRAL/SHORT are executable, and the five-tier rating is advisory. `extract_protective_price` pulls the first absolute price from free-text guidance and deliberately returns None for percentages or qualitative text, because a protective order must never be submitted from an uncertain level.

sections.title: Action and position enums
sections.explanation: `AdvisoryRating` is the informational five-tier scale. `ExecutableAction` merges both trading modes' actions into one enum. `TargetPosition` and `PositionTransition` model the book state and every possible move between states, with `UNKNOWN` as a safe default.

sections.title: Trade intent building blocks
sections.explanation: `PlannedBrokerAction`, `RiskControls`, `ExecutionConstraints` and `OrderIntent` describe what the broker should do. Risk controls default to `advisory_only`, and `broker_protective_orders_enabled` defaults to False so stops are recorded but not submitted unless explicitly enabled. `TradeIntent` composes them with a schema version and timestamp as the execution contract.

sections.title: Agent output schemas
sections.explanation: `ResearchPlan`, `TraderProposal` and `RiskDecision` are the structured outputs requested from the Research Manager, Trader and Risk Manager via `with_structured_output`. Field descriptions double as instructions to the model. Optional fields such as stop loss and take profit stay as free text here; numeric levels are extracted later.

sections.title: Markdown renderers
sections.explanation: Each renderer turns a structured object into the Markdown report shown in the UI and stored in state. Optional fields are emitted only when present, and every renderer ends with `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL: **ACTION**`, so structured and free-text responses look the same to `extract_recommendation`.

sections.title: Position mapping helpers
sections.explanation: `trade_intent_action` reads the action from either a model or a plain dict. `_target_position` maps actions to the desired book state per mode; in investment mode SELL means go flat rather than short, and HOLD keeps the current position. `_position_transition` is a lookup table from (current, target) pairs to transitions.

sections.title: Planned actions and order intent
sections.explanation: Transitions are expanded into concrete broker steps: opens use market orders sized by configured notional, closes use `close_position` sized by the current position, and reversals emit a close followed by an open. Hold transitions yield a single no-order step. `_primary_order_intent` picks the last actionable step and sets time in force to `gtc` for crypto and `day` for equities.

sections.title: Building the trade intent
sections.explanation: `build_trade_intent_from_risk_decision` assembles the full contract. Crypto is detected by a `/` in the symbol; warnings are added for crypto shorts, disabled shorts, and risk controls without absolute prices. Broker protective orders are enabled only when a numeric stop or target was extracted and the asset is not crypto.

tradingagents/agents/trader/trader.py.overview: Factory for the Trader node, which turns the Research Manager's `investment_plan` into a concrete swing-trading proposal. It enriches the prompt with live Alpaca position and account data, mode-specific instructions, the compact evidence packet and memory, then requests a structured `TraderProposal` with several fallback passes. Its output `trader_investment_plan` feeds the risk debate. This is the main file of tour step 9.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports the `TraderProposal` schema, trading-mode helpers, decision memory, report-context helpers, structured-output utilities and `AlpacaUtils` for live broker data. The optional web UI prompt-capture hook falls back to a no-op.

sections.title: Live position and account snapshot
sections.explanation: Structured output is bound once at factory time. The node reads the live position from Alpaca and writes it into `state['current_position']` so downstream agents see the same view.
