It then formats the symbol's quantity, entry price and P/L (matching symbols with `/` stripped, for crypto) and an account summary with buying power and cash.

sections.title: Mode and evidence context
sections.explanation: `get_trading_mode_context` is called with the current position so trading mode can include position-transition logic. The context bundle is retrieved with the `trader` role, and the compact analysis packet is preferred when available. Everything is rendered into the `trader/trader_context` template that becomes part of the system message.

sections.title: Plan validation and message assembly
sections.explanation: If the incoming investment plan is too short (under 150 characters, or little more than a bare final line), the trader switches to an enhanced prompt built from the analysis packet instead of trusting a thin plan. Messages are built as a system plus user pair, and the combined text is captured for the UI with a fallback to the system message alone.

sections.title: Invocation with fallback passes
sections.explanation: The first call uses `invoke_structured_or_freetext`. If the result is too thin, a fallback-plan prompt is tried. If no `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL` appears, a dedicated final-decision prompt is run and its output is appended under a 'Final Trading Decision' heading rather than replacing the analysis.

sections.title: Final normalization and state output
sections.explanation: The recommendation is extracted; when none is found it defaults to the safe action for the mode (NEUTRAL or HOLD). `ensure_final_transaction_proposal` guarantees the canonical final line. The node returns the message, `trader_investment_plan`, mode, position and `recommended_action`, and `functools.partial` binds the node name 'Trader'.

tradingagents/agents/utils/agent_trading.overview: Central utilities for the two trading modes: investment mode (BUY/HOLD/SELL, no shorts) and trading mode (LONG/NEUTRAL/SHORT with position logic), selected by the `allow_shorts` config flag. It supplies mode-specific prompt context, extracts the final recommendation from agent text, and enforces the canonical final-proposal line. Every decision agent in tour step 9 and 10 relies on it.

sections.title: Mode definitions
sections.explanation: The docstring documents the two modes. `TradingModeConfig` is a plain namespace of action lists and position constants used for validation and fallback extraction.

sections.title: Building mode context
sections.explanation: `get_trading_mode_context` switches on `allow_shorts`. Both branches return a dict with the mode key, a display name, allowed actions, instructions rendered from external templates, and the exact `final_format` string that prompts ask the model to emit. Trading mode additionally renders `position_logic` for the current position.

sections.title: Agent-specific instructions
sections.explanation: Renders a `trading_modes/agent_context_<type>` template for each known agent type and returns the requested one, falling back to the base instructions for unknown types. Note that all five templates are rendered on every call even though only one is used.

sections.title: Extracting the recommendation
sections.explanation: The response is uppercased and matched against an ordered list of exact patterns such as `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL: **BUY**`, with trading mode also recognizing risk-management phrasing. As a fallback, a bolded action in the last 100 characters is accepted. Returning None lets callers apply their own safe default.

sections.title: Validation and transitions
sections.explanation: `validate_recommendation` checks an action belongs to the active mode. `get_position_transition` is a string-based table describing the move between current and new positions; unknown combinations return an `UNKNOWN` action instead of raising.

sections.title: Canonical final line
sections.explanation: `format_final_decision` produces the same `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL` format for both modes. `ensure_final_transaction_proposal` appends that line only if it is missing, preserving the analysis text, so downstream signal parsing always finds an exact, executable action.

tradingagents/agents/utils/structured.py.overview: Small helpers that make structured LLM output optional. They bind a Pydantic schema when the provider supports it and transparently fall back to a free-text call on any failure, so decision agents never break because a model or provider lacks structured output. Used by the Research Manager, Trader and Risk Manager in tour steps 9 and 10.

sections.title: Setup
sections.explanation: Declares a module logger and a type variable bound to `BaseModel` so render callbacks are typed against the schema.

sections.title: Binding a schema
sections.explanation: `bind_structured` calls `llm.with_structured_output(schema)` and returns None when the client lacks that method or raises `NotImplementedError`, logging a warning with the agent name. Callers bind once at factory time.

sections.title: Structured call with free-text fallback
sections.explanation: When a structured LLM exists, the parsed object is rendered to text. Any exception, such as a schema validation error, is logged and the same prompt is retried on the plain LLM. The return value is always a string, using `.content` when present.

sections.title: Returning the structured object
sections.explanation: A variant that returns both the rendered text and the parsed object, or None for the object on fallback. The Risk Manager uses it because it needs the structured `RiskDecision` to build a `TradeIntent`, not just Markdown.

tradingagents/agents/managers/risk_manag.overview: Factory for the Risk Manager node, the judge of the risky/safe/neutral risk debate and the final decision maker. It combines live Alpaca account data, mode context, the claim matrix, a risk-debate digest and memories, asks for a structured `RiskDecision`, and converts it into a machine-readable `final_trade_intent` for execution. This is the central file of tour step 10.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports `RiskDecision`, `ExecutableAction` and `build_trade_intent_from_risk_decision` from the schemas module, along with trading-mode, memory, report-context and structured-output helpers. Notably it uses `invoke_structured_object_or_freetext` so it can keep the parsed decision object.

sections.title: Live position and account data
sections.explanation: Reads `allow_shorts` from config, then fetches the live position and writes it into state. The position and account description blocks mirror the Trader's, so the judge sees the same broker snapshot. Note that `trader_plan` is read from `state['investment_plan']`.

sections.title: Context and prompt
sections.explanation: Uses the `manager` agent context and the `managers/risk_manager` evidence role, whose weights favor macro and market reports. `build_debate_digest(..., 'risk')` summarizes the latest risky, safe and neutral positions. The full prompt is captured as `final_trade_decision` for the UI.

sections.title: Decision and trade intent
sections.explanation: The structured call returns text plus an optional `RiskDecision`. If structured output was unavailable, a minimal decision is synthesized from the extracted action with confidence 'unknown' and an explicit note that stops and targets are not inferred from free text. The decision is then converted to a JSON-serializable `TradeIntent` that carries planned broker actions and warnings.

sections.title: Final state update
sections.explanation: The risk debate state is rebuilt with the judge decision and `latest_speaker` set to 'Judge'. The node returns the final Markdown decision, the `final_trade_intent`, the mode, the position and the recommended action for signal processing and execution.

tradingagents/portfolio/__init__.py.overview: Deterministic portfolio-level sizing that runs above the per-symbol agent decisions. It adjusts the notional of new long or short exposure with three arithmetic guards (correlation penalty, inverse-volatility sizing, gross exposure cap) and no LLM involvement. It is called at execution time and is part of the sizing story in tour step 10.

sections.title: Design rationale
sections.explanation: The docstring explains why this layer exists: agents analyze symbols in isolation. Only positive correlation is penalized because negative correlation is a hedge, inverse volatility is chosen over optimization for stability, and only the exposure cap may zero a trade. Missing price history skips penalties, but missing account exposure blocks entries.

sections.title: Config and verdict types
sections.explanation: `PortfolioLimitsConfig` holds the thresholds, and `from_config` maps `portfolio_*` keys from the main config, ignoring None values so defaults survive. `PortfolioVerdict` records the requested and adjusted notional, per-symbol correlations, applied factors and human-readable reasons.

sections.title: Return and volatility helpers
sections.explanation: `daily_returns` accepts either a close series or an OHLCV frame, normalizes column names, deduplicates timestamps and computes close-to-close returns. `realized_daily_vol` returns 0.0 when undefined, and `_candidate_returns` returns None on short or malformed data so callers can skip statistics.

sections.title: Correlation and volatility penalties
sections.explanation: `assess_new_position` validates inputs, then correlates the candidate against each open position over aligned bars. The correlation sign is flipped for shorts and for short holdings, so the penalty reflects whether the new exposure duplicates existing risk. Above the threshold, size is scaled by the correlated factor; realized volatility above target scales by target over realized. The combined factor is floored at `min_size_factor` so penalties cannot shrink a trade to dust.

sections.title: Gross exposure cap
sections.explanation: Headroom is equity times the cap percentage minus current gross exposure, and the adjusted notional is clipped to it. If equity is unavailable while a cap is configured, new exposure is blocked entirely. `allowed` is simply whether any notional remains.

sections.title: Execution-time hook
sections.explanation: `adjust_new_position_notional` only touches BUY, LONG and SHORT; closing or holding actions pass through untouched. Shorts are assessed with side 'sell'. Any exception from gathering state or assessment fails closed by returning 0.0, blocking new exposure while closes still work.

sections.title: Gathering state from Alpaca
sections.explanation: Alpaca imports are lazy so the package stays importable without the data stack. Positions are keyed with `/` removed, and crypto positions are mapped back to `XXX/USD` data symbols. A bar requirement is converted to calendar days with a holiday buffer, and failed price downloads are skipped rather than aborting.

tradingagents/regime.py.overview: Deterministic market-regime detection over volatility, trend and liquidity using fixed thresholds rather than a fitted model. The result is a filter, not a signal: hostile regimes shrink position size through floored multipliers but never flip agent decisions, and missing data reads as unknown with a neutral multiplier. It feeds both the market analyst report and execution-time sizing, as described in tour step 10.

sections.title: Design rationale
sections.explanation: Explains why threshold rules were chosen over an HMM (no fitting, no initialization sensitivity, no new dependency) and names the two failure-isolated integration points: a Markdown block for the market report and a sizing multiplier.

sections.title: Regime configuration
sections.explanation: `RegimeConfig` defines windows, percentile thresholds, an absolute annualized volatility floor, liquidity ratios, size factors and a minimum multiplier. `from_config` maps `regime_*` config keys onto fields.

sections.title: Assessment and Markdown output
sections.explanation: `RegimeAssessment` stores the three states, an overall label, the multiplier and metrics. `to_markdown` renders a section that only shows metric details when available and ends by telling downstream agents to treat it as risk context, not a trade signal.

sections.title: Normalization and volatility state
sections.explanation: `_normalize` lowercases columns, indexes by timestamp and adds a zero volume column if missing. `classify_regime` returns an unknown assessment on bad or short data. Volatility is the 20-bar rolling standard deviation, annualized with 365 periods for crypto (symbols containing `/`) or 252 for equities, ranked against its own history; the absolute floor catches assets that are always volatile.

sections.title: Trend and liquidity states
sections.explanation: Trend compares price to its SMA and the SMA's slope over a few bars, yielding up, down or sideways. Liquidity uses share volume rather than dollar volume to avoid double-counting price declines, and the baseline window strictly precedes the recent window so a slow bleed cannot drag its own baseline down.

sections.title: Multiplier and label
sections.explanation: Factors for turbulence, downtrend and thinning liquidity multiply together and are floored at `min_risk_multiplier`. The label is hostile for turbulence or down trend with thinning liquidity, favorable for an uptrend in calm or normal volatility, otherwise mixed. A favorable regime always uses a multiplier of 1.0.

sections.title: Loading price history
sections.explanation: The default loader is imported lazily from `AlpacaUtils`. The required bar count is converted into calendar days with a buffer, and bars after the `as_of_date` cutoff are filtered out to avoid look-ahead. Undated history is rejected.

sections.title: Integration points
sections.explanation: `regime_report_block` returns Markdown, or an empty string when the regime is unknown or loading fails. `regime_risk_multiplier` returns the multiplier and logs when sizing is reduced; any failure returns 1.0 so the regime filter never blocks a trade on its own.

tradingagents/risk/position_sizing.py.overview: Pure, deterministic position sizing: fractional Kelly allocation, ATR-based stops, a risk-per-trade budget and exposure caps. No broker or LLM calls are made, so behavior is unit-testable and independent of model quality. The module's principle is that the LLM decides direction and this layer decides size, which is the sizing half of tour step 10.

sections.title: Defaults and edge assumptions
sections.explanation: `DEFAULT_CONFIDENCE_EDGE` maps the LLM's high/medium/low confidence to conservative (win rate, win/loss ratio) estimates, deliberately assuming only a slight edge because Kelly sizing is fragile to estimation error. `FALLBACK_STOP_PCT` is the default stop distance when ATR is unavailable.

sections.title: Wilder ATR
sections.explanation: `compute_atr` resolves high/low/close columns case-insensitively, builds the true range, seeds with a simple average and then applies Wilder smoothing. It returns None for missing columns, short history, NaNs or non-positive results so callers can fall back instead of crashing.

sections.title: Fractional Kelly
sections.explanation: Implements Kelly % = W - (1 - W) / R scaled by `kelly_fraction` (half-Kelly by default). Invalid or edge-free inputs return 0.0, meaning do not allocate, rather than raising.

sections.title: Parameters and decision types
sections.explanation: `RiskParameters` is a frozen dataclass with strict defaults: 1 percent risk per trade, a 2x ATR stop, a 20 percent single-position cap and an 80 percent gross exposure cap. `from_dict` ignores unknown keys. `SizingDecision` records approval, notional, stop price, risk amount and which caps bound, and `_rejection` builds a zero-size decision with a reason.

sections.title: Input validation and stop distance
sections.explanation: `PositionSizer.size_position` validates every numeric input and parameter for finiteness and positivity, rejecting rather than guessing. Stop distance comes from ATR times the multiplier, or a percentage of price with an `atr_unavailable_default_stop` note. If remaining exposure room is below the minimum notional, the trade is rejected up front.

sections.title: Applying caps and computing the stop
sections.explanation: Five caps are computed: the requested notional, the risk-per-trade notional (risk budget divided by stop distance, times price), the Kelly notional, the single-position cap and the exposure room. The minimum wins, and every cap equal to it is reported as binding. The notional is floored to cents, and the stop price is placed above entry for sells or shorts and below it for buys.

tradingagents/alerts.py.overview: Operational alerting for the trading system, sending messages to Telegram and/or a generic JSON webhook using only the standard library. It is called by the safety layer when orders are blocked or the kill switch is engaged, which makes it the last piece of the 'Safe Execution on Alpaca' tour step. The module's three design rules (deduplication, isolation from trading, secret hygiene) are stated in its docstring and enforced in code.

sections.title: Design rules and module state
sections.explanation: The docstring records the three rules the module obeys: dedupe repeated alerts with a cooldown, never let alert failures affect trading, and never echo the Telegram token. A module-level `_LAST_SENT` dict guarded by `_DEDUPE_LOCK` holds the last successful send time per dedupe key, so the cooldown is process-wide and thread-safe.

sections.title: AlertConfig dataclass
sections.explanation: `AlertConfig` gathers the toggle, Telegram bot token and chat id, webhook URL and cooldown. `from_config` reads `alert_*` keys from the runtime config and falls back to `ALERT_*` environment variables, so credentials can live outside the config file. `reset_alert_dedupe` clears the cooldown map for tests and manual operations.

sections.title: HTTP transport
sections.explanation: `_post_json` is a minimal POST of a JSON body via `urllib.request` with a 10-second timeout. It is the default transport, and `send_alert` lets tests inject a different callable instead of hitting the network.

sections.title: send_alert dispatcher
sections.explanation: Checks the cooldown under the lock and returns early with `deduped=True` if the same key was sent recently. Each configured channel is tried independently inside its own `try/except`; failures print only the exception type, deliberately suppressing the URL because the Telegram URL embeds the bot token. The cooldown timestamp is recorded only after at least one channel succeeded, so a failed delivery does not silence the next attempt. The function never raises and reports results in a dict.

sections.title: Safety-specific helpers
sections.explanation: `notify_safety_block` keys its dedupe on the sorted list of block reasons rather than the symbol, so a tripped circuit breaker produces one alert per cooldown window regardless of how many orders it blocks. `notify_kill_switch` uses a fixed key so engaging the kill switch repeatedly alerts once per window.

tradingagents/dataflows/alpaca_utils.py.overview: The single gateway to the Alpaca broker and market-data APIs: it builds clients, fetches bars and quotes (with an optional yfinance fallback), reads account and position state, and — most importantly — turns a validated trade decision into real orders. In the 'Safe Execution on Alpaca' tour step this is where the typed TradeIntent is checked, re-sized by the deterministic risk engine, gated by the safety layer, and submitted with optional bracket/OTO protection. Many functions intentionally fail closed for execution paths while failing soft for UI and prompt paths.

sections.title: Imports and entry-order serialization
sections.explanation: Imports the alpaca-py data and trading clients plus the deterministic position sizer. `TradeIntent` is only imported under `TYPE_CHECKING` to avoid a circular dataflows-agents import. `_submit_entry_order` holds a process-wide lock while checking for an existing open order on the symbol and raises `PendingEntryError` if one exists, preventing duplicate entries from concurrent loops or restarts.

sections.title: Fallback data and asset search helpers
sections.explanation: A hard-coded ticker-to-company map provides names when the API cannot. `_ASSET_SEARCH_CACHE` and the `_asset_to_search_result`/`_fallback_asset_results` helpers normalize Alpaca asset objects into plain dicts for the WebUI symbol picker, with a static fallback list when the broker is unreachable.

sections.title: Client factories
sections.explanation: Factories for the stock-data, crypto-data and trading clients read keys via `get_api_key`. Stock and trading clients require credentials and raise a clear error otherwise, while the crypto client works keyless (keys only raise rate limits). The trading client defaults to paper trading unless the config explicitly says false/0/no — a safe default for a trading bot.

sections.title: Timeframe parsing and yfinance fallback
sections.explanation: `_parse_timeframe` maps strings like '5Min', '4h' or '1Day' to alpaca TimeFrame objects, defaulting to daily. `_is_supported_data_fallback_error` classifies errors (subscription, auth, rate limit, timeout, empty) that justify falling back, and `_yfinance_fallback_data` fetches daily or hourly bars from Yahoo only when `data_fallback_enabled` is on, normalizing columns to the same OHLCV schema. Minute data is never faked from Yahoo.

sections.title: Asset search and historical bars
sections.explanation: `search_assets` ranks cached assets by exact symbol, prefix, name and substring matches, with tweaks favoring USD crypto quotes and tradable assets. `get_stock_data` picks the crypto or stock client by the '/' in the symbol, requests bars, filters to the symbol, and trims the bar at the exclusive end boundary so the inclusive end date does not leak the next day's midnight bar. On recognized errors it tries the yfinance fallback, otherwise returns an empty frame.

sections.title: Quotes, windows and account read models
sections.explanation: Read-only helpers used by agents and the WebUI: latest bid/ask quote, a look-back window of bars, company names, formatted positions with P/L, paginated recent orders and account cash/buying power. These all swallow errors and return empty or zero values, which is acceptable for display but is exactly why execution code uses stricter functions below.

sections.title: Position state and order primitives
sections.explanation: `get_current_position_state` maps the live position to LONG/SHORT/NEUTRAL; its `strict` flag makes execution callers re-raise on outages or non-finite quantities, because a guessed NEUTRAL could re-buy an existing holding or skip a real exit. `place_market_order` chooses GTC for crypto and DAY for equities; `place_protected_market_order` builds a BRACKET (stop and target) or OTO (single leg) whole-share order; `close_position` validates the percentage and closes fully or partially. Entry orders go through `_submit_entry_order`.

sections.title: Risk snapshot and deterministic sizing
sections.explanation: `get_account_risk_snapshot` raises rather than returning zeros when equity or exposure is invalid, since a silent zero would corrupt sizing. `compute_risk_sized_amount` combines that snapshot with a mid quote (or last close) and ATR from recent bars, then delegates to `PositionSizer` so the dollar size is computed mathematically rather than taken from the LLM.

sections.title: execute_trade_intent and protective prices
sections.explanation: Validates the TradeIntent with Pydantic, checks the symbol matches, resolves the action and verifies it is legal for the trading mode, and rejects shorts for crypto or when disabled. For position-opening actions it re-sizes via the risk engine (blocking new exposure if sizing fails), resolves broker-side stop/target levels via `_resolve_protective_prices` (rejecting inverted levels and crypto), and can inject the risk engine's ATR stop. After execution it labels the protective status (bracket, OTO, failed or advisory-only). `_safety_context` fetches equity and position value for the circuit breakers.

sections.title: execute_trading_action state machine
sections.explanation: The final gate before the broker. Nested helpers run the SafetyGuard immediately before each order: closes are passed as risk-reducing so a loss breaker cannot trap a position, while new exposure is blocked if the guard or account data is unavailable. Quantities are derived only from a real quote, a failed protected order is never retried as an unprotected one, and position flips wait for the close to be filled. Results feed the guard's consecutive-rejection counter and blocked orders trigger a deduplicated alert.

tradingagents/graph/signal_processing.py.overview: A small component that reduces the final, verbose trading decision text to a single action keyword such as BUY, SELL, HOLD, LONG, SHORT or NEUTRAL. It is the bridge between the LLM-written decision and the execution layer described in the 'Safe Execution on Alpaca' tour step. Deterministic parsing is tried first so most runs need no extra LLM call.

sections.title: Imports and constructor
sections.explanation: Imports the LangChain chat model type and the prompt loader. The processor stores the quick-thinking LLM, which is only used as a last-resort fallback.

sections.title: Deterministic extraction
sections.explanation: Upper-cases the signal and looks for the exact `FINAL TRANSACTION PROPOSAL: **ACTION**` marker, checking trading-mode words before investment-mode words. If that marker is missing, it scans the last 100 characters for any action keyword. This keeps extraction cheap, reproducible and free of model variance in the common case.

sections.title: LLM fallback
sections.explanation: Only when no keyword is found does it send the full text to the LLM with the externally stored `graph/signal_extraction_system` prompt, then strips and upper-cases the reply. Note the result is not validated against an allowed set here; downstream execution code is responsible for rejecting unexpected actions.

tradingagents/safety/guardrails.py.overview: The deterministic production safety layer that every outbound order must pass. It contains pure arithmetic checks — per-order notional cap, per-symbol concentration cap, daily-loss, drawdown and rejection-streak circuit breakers — plus a file-based kill switch and a daily LLM token budget. It deliberately makes no LLM calls and imports nothing from the agent stack, so a model cannot argue its way past a halt; this is the core of the 'Safe Execution on Alpaca' tour step.

sections.title: Design notes and defaults
sections.explanation: The docstring explains the three stages (pre-trade checks, circuit breakers, kill switch) and the token budget. `DEFAULT_SAFETY_CONFIG` pulls only the safety keys from `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, and state lives under `~/.tradingagents/safety`.

sections.title: Verdict type and defensive parsing
sections.explanation: `SafetyVerdict` carries an allowed flag, human-readable reasons and a per-check status map. `_finite_float` treats NaN, infinity and unparseable values as unavailable, because a NaN that reaches a comparison silently passes every breaker and a NaN high-water mark would disable drawdown protection permanently.

sections.title: SafetyGuard construction and persistence
sections.explanation: The guard merges user config over defaults, uses an RLock for thread safety and loads a small JSON state file (high-water mark, rejection streak, per-day token counts). `_save_state` writes to a temp file and uses `os.replace` for an atomic swap so a crash cannot leave a half-written state file.

sections.title: Kill switch
sections.explanation: The kill switch is simply the existence of a flag file, so operators can engage it with `touch` without Python. Engaging writes the reason and timestamp and sends an alert via a lazily imported, failure-isolated call, keeping the safety layer free of hard dependencies.

sections.title: Rejection streak and LLM budget
sections.explanation: `record_order_result` resets or increments the consecutive-rejection counter that serves as a data or connectivity glitch signal. Token usage is accumulated per day (keeping only the last 31 days), and `check_llm_budget` refuses new analyses once the daily budget is exhausted.

sections.title: check_order pre-trade gate
sections.explanation: The main gate. The kill switch is checked first and blocks everything. Risk-reducing exits skip all exposure and breaker checks so a loss halt cannot trap an open position. Otherwise it evaluates the notional cap, concentration versus equity, daily loss versus last equity, drawdown versus a persisted high-water mark (updated as equity rises) and the rejection streak. Checks lacking account data are reported as skipped rather than guessed, and the verdict is allowed only if no reasons accumulated.

sections.title: Dashboard status
sections.explanation: `status` runs a zero-notional check plus the budget check and converts them into a green/red map for the WebUI safety panel, along with the kill-switch state and effective config.

sections.title: Process-wide singleton
sections.explanation: `get_safety_guard` lazily builds one guard per process from the runtime config, importing the dataflows config lazily so the safety module stays importable even when that stack is broken. `reset_safety_guard` clears it for tests or config reloads.

tradingagents/agents/utils/memory.py.overview: Holds the two memory mechanisms that make the agents learn from past outcomes. `FinancialSituationMemory` is a ChromaDB vector store of (situation, lesson) pairs retrieved by embedding similarity, and `TradingMemoryLog` is an append-only Markdown log of final decisions whose outcomes are filled in later. Both are central to the 'Auditing, Memory and Reflection' tour step and include safeguards against lookahead when replaying history.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Brings in ChromaDB, the OpenAI client for embeddings, date utilities and the recommendation extractor used by the decision log.

sections.title: Vector memory setup and embeddings
sections.explanation: The constructor uses a persistent ChromaDB client when `agent_memory_dir` is configured, which makes reflection lessons survive restarts; otherwise memory is in-process only. `get_embedding` truncates very long text by keeping its head and tail, and on the first embedding failure disables embeddings for the rest of the run with a single warning instead of crashing.

sections.title: Adding lessons
sections.explanation: `add_situations` embeds each situation and stores the lesson in metadata with random UUID ids, since count-based ids would collide across processes sharing a persistent collection. Each entry gets `created_at` (overridable) and an `available_at_ts` timestamp recording when the lesson really became known. `has_metadata_value` supports idempotent batch teaching.

sections.title: Retrieving lessons
sections.explanation: `get_memories` queries by embedding similarity and returns matched situations, recommendations and a similarity score. When an `as_of_date` in the past is given, it filters on `available_at_ts`, so historical replays cannot see lessons learned after that date; legacy entries without this field are excluded.

sections.title: Example usage
sections.explanation: A `__main__` demo that adds sample situations and queries them. Note it calls `FinancialSituationMemory()` without the required `name` argument, so it is illustrative rather than runnable as-is.

sections.title: Decision log: storing and loading
sections.explanation: `TradingMemoryLog` appends entries tagged `[date | ticker | action | rating | pending]`, separated by an HTML comment marker, and skips duplicates for the same pending date and ticker. `get_past_context` returns recent resolved entries for the same ticker in full plus short cross-ticker reflections, and returns nothing for past `as_of_date` values because the log lacks availability timestamps.

sections.title: Resolving outcomes and rotation
sections.explanation: `batch_update_with_outcomes` rewrites matching pending tags with raw return, alpha and holding days, appends a REFLECTION section, and writes atomically via a temp file. `_apply_rotation` drops the oldest resolved entries beyond `memory_log_max_entries` while always keeping pending ones.

sections.title: Parsing and formatting helpers
sections.explanation: `_parse_entry` splits the tag line into fields and extracts DECISION and REFLECTION bodies with regexes. The formatters render full entries or compact reflection-only summaries for prompts, and `_extract_advisory_rating` pulls an 'advisory rating' line from the decision text.

tradingagents/graph/checkpointer.py.overview: Optional LangGraph checkpointing backed by SQLite, letting an interrupted analysis for a ticker and date resume instead of restarting. Each ticker gets its own database file and each (ticker, date) pair maps to a stable thread id. It belongs to the 'Auditing, Memory and Reflection' tour step as part of run durability.

sections.title: Paths and thread ids
sections.explanation: `_db_path` sanitizes the ticker and places one SQLite file per ticker under `<data_dir>/checkpoints`. `thread_id` hashes `TICKER:date` with SHA-256 and truncates it, giving a deterministic id so a rerun of the same analysis finds the same checkpoint.

sections.title: Optional dependency loading
sections.explanation: The SqliteSaver class is imported lazily and a missing `langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite` package produces an actionable error message, so the feature is opt-in and does not break installs without it.

sections.title: Checkpointer context manager
sections.explanation: `get_checkpointer` opens a SQLite connection with `check_same_thread=False`, wraps it in a SqliteSaver, runs `setup()` to create tables, and always closes the connection afterwards.

sections.title: Inspecting and clearing checkpoints
sections.explanation: `checkpoint_step` reads the latest checkpoint's step from metadata, and `has_checkpoint` wraps it as a boolean. `clear_checkpoint` deletes rows for one thread id from the known tables, tolerating missing tables, while `clear_all_checkpoints` removes every database file and returns how many were deleted.

tradingagents/graph/reflection.py.overview: The `Reflector` turns realized trade outcomes into written lessons and stores them in each agent's vector memory. It reflects on the bull and bear researchers, trader, investment judge and risk manager separately, and can also write a compact reflection for the decision log. This is the learning loop described in the 'Auditing, Memory and Reflection' tour step.

sections.title: Setup and situation extraction
sections.explanation: The reflector loads its system prompt from the external template `graph/reflection_system`. `_extract_current_situation` concatenates the market, sentiment, news and fundamentals reports, which become the situation key that lessons are embedded under.

sections.title: Generic component reflection
sections.explanation: `_reflect_on_component` renders the `graph/reflection_component_human` template with the returns, the component's report and the situation, then calls the quick LLM. The `component_type` argument is accepted but not used in the prompt.

sections.title: Per-agent reflections
sections.explanation: Five near-identical methods pick the relevant text from the final state (debate histories, trader plan, judge decisions), generate a reflection and add `(situation, lesson)` to that agent's memory. Using the same situation text for storage and retrieval is what lets agents later recall lessons from similar markets.

sections.title: reflect_on_outcome orchestrator
sections.explanation: Runs every per-agent reflection for which a memory was supplied. Each is wrapped in its own try/except so one missing state key or LLM error does not prevent the other lessons from being written, and a per-component success map is returned.

sections.title: Final-decision reflection
sections.explanation: Formats raw and alpha returns as signed percentages and renders the final-memory prompts to produce a short reflection for `TradingMemoryLog`. It also serves the backtest teaching bridge, which passes `alpha_return=None`.

tradingagents/run_logger.py.overview: The run audit logger that records every analysis run as a JSON file under `eval_results/<symbol>/TradingAgentsStrategy_logs/runs/`. It captures prompts, tool calls, LLM calls, agent outputs and state snapshots incrementally, so partial runs remain debuggable. Its files are later the data source for reflection and backtesting, which is why it opens the 'Auditing, Memory and Reflection' tour step.

sections.title: Serialization and redaction helpers
sections.explanation: `_sanitize_for_path` makes symbols safe for directory names, and `_json_safe` recursively coerces values to JSON-serializable forms, falling back to `str`. `_redact_sensitive_config` replaces credentials (API keys, secrets, tokens, webhook URLs, chat ids) with `[REDACTED]` before a config is persisted, so audit files never leak secrets.

sections.title: Logger lifecycle and crash recovery
sections.explanation: On construction the logger scans existing run files and marks any left in `running` state as `aborted`, recovering from previous crashes. It also registers an `atexit` hook that closes in-flight runs with an error note; that hook swallows all exceptions because exit handlers must never raise.

sections.title: Starting a run
sections.explanation: `start_run` creates a unique run id from the trade date, wall time and a short UUID, initializes the summary counters and writes the file immediately. `_resolve_run_id` lets callers log by run id, by symbol, or implicitly when only one run is active.

sections.title: Event logging and counters
sections.explanation: `log_event` appends a timestamped event and updates summary counters by type: prompt characters, tool time and suspect outputs, LLM latency, characters and tokens, and error counts. LLM token totals are also forwarded to the safety guard's daily budget inside a try/except so logging never fails because of the guard. The file is flushed after every event.

sections.title: Typed logging wrappers and snapshots
sections.explanation: `log_prompt`, `log_tool_call` and `log_agent_output` are thin wrappers that build consistent payloads for `log_event`. `log_state_snapshot` stores named state snapshots under `snapshots`.

sections.title: Finishing and flushing
sections.explanation: `finish_run` sets the end time and status, stores the final state and final signal, records any error, flushes and removes the run from the active maps. `_flush_unlocked` rewrites the whole JSON file and must be called while holding the lock.

sections.title: Snapshot lookup and singleton
sections.explanation: `load_final_state_snapshot` returns the final state of the newest completed run for a symbol and date, letting reflection recover the exact situation a past decision was made in. A module-level singleton is created at import time (which triggers stale-log recovery) and exposed via `get_run_audit_logger`.

tradingagents/backtest/engine.py.overview: A walk-forward backtesting engine built on backtrader that replays dated agent decisions against historical OHLCV bars. Orders are placed at a bar's close and fill at the next bar's open, avoiding lookahead bias, and slippage plus commission are applied by default. It is the main file of the 'Backtesting Recorded Decisions' tour step, with helpers that pull signals from recorded runs at zero LLM cost.

sections.title: Module contract and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring states the key discipline: a decision made on day t cannot benefit from day t's own price because fills happen at the next open. Metrics and signal helpers are imported from sibling modules, and `_BPS` defines one basis point.

sections.title: Volatility-scaled slippage broker
sections.explanation: A custom backtrader broker whose slippage percentage is a fraction of the previous completed bar's high-low range relative to its close, clamped between min and max basis points. It overrides `_slip_up`/`_slip_down` to set `slip_perc` dynamically before delegating, and uses only the prior bar so no intrabar knowledge is needed.

sections.title: Signal replay strategy
sections.explanation: `_SignalReplayStrategy` records equity each bar and consumes all signals dated on or before the current bar, so weekend or holiday signals apply on the next trading day rather than being dropped. BUY targets a fixed portfolio fraction, SELL closes longs, NEUTRAL flattens, SHORT opens shorts only when allowed, and HOLD does nothing. Completed, margin and rejected orders and closed-trade PnL are captured for reporting.

sections.title: Result dataclasses
sections.explanation: `BacktestResult` holds the equity curve, trade PnLs, orders, metrics, date range, rejected orders and slippage config, with a JSON-friendly `to_dict`. `WalkForwardResult` holds per-window metrics plus the full-period result.

sections.title: Price frame validation
sections.explanation: `normalize_price_frame` lower-cases columns, indexes by timestamp, strips timezones and validates the data strictly: required columns, finite values, positive prices, non-negative volume and OHLC consistency. Duplicate timestamps keep the last row and the frame is sorted, so bad data fails loudly instead of producing misleading results.

sections.title: run_backtest
sections.explanation: Validates parameters, normalizes every signal date and action (raising on unknown actions) and drops signals after the last bar. It then wires up Cerebro with the chosen slippage model ('fixed' by default at 5 bps, 'volatility' or 'none'), cash, commission and the replay strategy, and summarizes the resulting equity curve with the metrics module.

sections.title: Walk-forward evaluation
sections.explanation: Splits the price history into consecutive non-overlapping windows (63 bars by default), each restarting with fresh capital. Since LLM replay has no parameters to refit, the goal is robustness: per-window metrics reveal regime dependence. A short trailing remainder is folded into the last window, and a full-period backtest is also returned.

sections.title: Recorded-signal entry points
sections.explanation: `run_recorded_backtest` and `run_recorded_walk_forward` load signals from persisted run logs, drop signals that predate the requested start, fetch prices via `AlpacaUtils.get_stock_data` (or an injected loader) and choose 365 periods per year for crypto symbols versus 252 for equities.

tradingagents/backtest/metrics.py.overview: Pure-math performance metrics for backtests: cumulative and annualized return, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown and win rate. The functions have no network, broker or LLM dependencies, so every number shown in the UI can be reproduced in a unit test. They follow the metric set of the TradingAgents paper and support the 'Backtesting Recorded Decisions' tour step.

sections.title: Constants and coercion
sections.explanation: Defines 252 trading days per year for equities and 365 for crypto, and `_as_series` converts any sequence to a float Series so all functions accept lists or pandas objects.

sections.title: Return metrics
sections.explanation: `cumulative_return` is final over initial equity minus one, returning None for short or non-positive curves. `annualized_return` is geometric, assumes one point per period and returns -100% if equity was wiped out.

sections.title: Sharpe ratio
sections.explanation: Converts the annual risk-free rate to a per-period rate, computes excess returns and annualizes mean over sample standard deviation by the square root of periods per year. It returns None rather than a fabricated number when the curve is too short or volatility is zero.

sections.title: Drawdown and win rate
sections.explanation: `max_drawdown` is the largest decline from the running peak, expressed as a positive fraction. `win_rate` is the share of closed trades with positive net PnL, or None when there are no trades.

sections.title: Summary
sections.explanation: `summarize_performance` bundles all metrics with trade count, period count and final equity into one dict that the engine and UI consume. Undefined values stay None.

tradingagents/backtest/signals.py.overview: Loads trading signals for backtesting from run logs the agent pipeline already wrote, so evaluating past behavior costs no LLM calls. It enforces strict timing rules: only completed runs that finished on their own analysis date (in the market's session timezone) count, which keeps later historical reruns from contaminating out-of-sample results. It feeds both the engine and the teaching bridge in the 'Backtesting Recorded Decisions' tour step.

sections.title: Purpose and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring explains the zero-cost replay idea and that normalization preserves the difference between exiting, holding and shorting.

sections.title: Action normalization
sections.explanation: `ACTION_ALIASES` maps LONG to BUY while keeping SELL, SHORT, HOLD and NEUTRAL distinct, and `normalize_action` returns None for anything unrecognized so callers can reject bad signals.

sections.title: Path sanitization
sections.explanation: Mirrors the run logger's path sanitizer instead of importing it, because importing `run_logger` would trigger its stale-log recovery side effect.

sections.title: load_recorded_runs
sections.explanation: Scans the symbol's run JSON files and keeps completed runs with a valid trade date and recognizable final signal. It requires timezone-aware start and end timestamps and that the run ended on the analysis date in New York time for equities or UTC for crypto; otherwise the run is excluded and counted. When several runs exist for one date the latest qualifying completion wins, and a warning reports how many were excluded.

sections.title: load_recorded_signals
sections.explanation: A convenience wrapper that turns the selected runs into a `{date: action}` map consumed by the backtest engine.

tradingagents/backtest/teach.py.overview: The bridge from backtesting to self-learning memory, called 'intensive teaching'. It replays recorded decisions against prices, computes a hypothetical fixed-horizon outcome for each, and writes one dated lesson per decision into the five agents' persistent ChromaDB memories so a fresh deployment starts with its own history. It closes the 'Backtesting Recorded Decisions' tour step by connecting it back to the memory and reflection loop.

sections.title: Design notes and report keys
sections.explanation: The docstring stresses next-open entry, that returns are hypothetical and before costs, and that teaching is idempotent via a `teach_key` and tagged `source=backtest_teach`. `_REPORT_KEYS` lists the analyst reports used to rebuild the situation text.

sections.title: compute_decision_outcomes
sections.explanation: For each signal it finds the first bar on or after the decision date, enters at the next bar's open and exits at the open `horizon_bars` later, flagging `partial` if data ends early. BUY earns the asset move and SHORT its negation; SELL, NEUTRAL and HOLD get no inferred return because position and cost history are unknown.

sections.title: Lesson text and memory construction
sections.explanation: `_situation_from_state` joins the stored analyst reports, matching how live reflection keys lessons. `_deterministic_lesson` writes a cautious template lesson that warns one observation does not establish an edge. `default_agent_memories` creates the five memories with the exact names the live graph uses, importing lazily so the backtest package stays importable without the agent stack.

sections.title: teach_memories_from_history
sections.explanation: Loads recorded runs, filters by date range, fetches prices and computes outcomes. For each outcome it skips memories that already hold the teach key, uses the final state of the exact run that produced the signal, and generates a lesson with the LLM reflector when given (and a return exists) or the deterministic template otherwise. Lessons are stored with rich metadata, and a decision only counts as taught if the collection actually grew, since embeddings may be unavailable.

run_webui_dash.py.overview: Command-line launcher for the Dash web UI. It parses server options, picks a free port starting from the requested one, and hands control to `webui.app_dash.run_app`. It is the process entry point used both locally and by the Docker image's `CMD`, which makes it the first stop of the Dash Web UI tour step.

sections.title: Imports and app hook
sections.explanation: A shebang and docstring, then standard-library imports plus the single project import, `run_app`. Importing `run_app` (not `app`) matters: `webui.app_dash` builds the Dash app lazily, so importing this function does not construct the component tree.

sections.title: Free-port discovery
sections.explanation: `find_available_port` scans up to 100 ports after the start port and tries to `bind` a TCP socket on `localhost` for each. The first successful bind wins and the socket is closed immediately by the context manager. Note that the probe binds to `localhost` even when the server later listens on another interface (for example `0.0.0.0` in Docker), so it is a best-effort check, and there is a small race window between probing and the real server binding.

sections.title: Argument parsing
sections.explanation: Defines `--port` (default 7860), `--share`, `--server-name` (default `127.0.0.1`, loopback only), `--debug` and `--max-threads`. The loopback default keeps the trading dashboard private unless the operator opts in; the Dockerfile overrides it with `0.0.0.0` inside the container while docker-compose still publishes only on host loopback.

sections.title: main and port fallback
sections.explanation: `main` resolves the port, exits with status 1 if nothing in the range is free, and prints a notice when it had to fall back to a different port. It then calls `run_app` with all options and passes its return value to `sys.exit`, so the process exit code reflects the server's return code.

webui/app_dash.py.overview: Builds and runs the Dash application: it creates a Flask server, wraps it in a Dash app with local Bootstrap assets, installs the layout from `webui/layout.py`, and registers all callbacks. It also monkey-patches `AppState.process_chunk_updates` with a report-mapping fix, and exposes the app lazily through a module-level `__getattr__`. In the tour's Dash Web UI step this is the assembly point between the launcher and the layout/state modules.

sections.title: Module docstring and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring records a past fix for multi-symbol pagination after page refresh. Imports bring in Dash, Bootstrap components, Flask, and the three project pieces the app is composed from: `APP_CONFIG` constants, `create_main_layout`, and `register_all_callbacks`.

sections.title: Sequential-mode report fix
sections.explanation: `apply_sequential_mode_fix` wraps `AppState.process_chunk_updates` at class level. When the Social Analyst is `in_progress` and a chunk carries `market_report` but no `sentiment_report`, it renames the key to `sentiment_report` before delegating to the original method, guarding against a mis-routed report overwriting the market analysis. A `_mapping_fix_applied` flag makes the patch idempotent, and any failure is reported but never prevents the app from starting. The leftover `chunk_fields`/`sentiment_length` variables are vestiges of commented-out debug prints.

sections.title: create_app factory
sections.explanation: Applies the patch, creates a Flask server, and constructs `dash.Dash` with the package's `assets` folder. `assets_ignore` stops Dash from auto-loading the vendored Bootstrap/FontAwesome CSS, and the local `/assets/vendor/bootstrap.min.css` is instead listed explicitly in `external_stylesheets` so load order is controlled and no CDN is required. Title, callback-exception suppression, and update-title settings come from `APP_CONFIG`; then the layout is set and callbacks are registered.

sections.title: run_app server loop
sections.explanation: Creates the app, quiets Werkzeug request logs and Dash callback logging, and calls `app.run` on the given host and port. Hot reload follows `debug`, but `use_reloader=False` prevents the Flask reloader from spawning a second process that would start background analysis threads twice. The `share` and `max_threads` arguments are accepted for CLI compatibility but are not used here. It returns 0 so the launcher can pass it to `sys.exit`.

sections.title: Lazy app attribute
sections.explanation: A PEP 562 module `__getattr__` builds the app only when someone accesses `webui.app_dash.app` (for example a WSGI host or a test), caching it in `_app`. This keeps plain imports cheap and side-effect free. Running the module directly starts the server in debug mode.

webui/components/analysis.py.overview: The bridge between the Dash UI and the trading graph. `start_analysis` validates UI inputs and enforces the LLM budget, `run_analysis` builds a config, streams `TradingAgentsGraph` chunks into the shared `app_state`, and records audit logs and memory, and `execute_trade_after_analysis` turns the final decision into Alpaca orders through portfolio, regime and position safety layers. It ties the Dash Web UI step to the graph, risk and execution steps of the tour.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Pulls in the graph, checkpoint cleanup, config access, the run audit logger, Alpaca execution helpers, and the two decision parsers (`trade_intent_action` for typed intents and `extract_recommendation` for legacy text). `app_state` is the process-wide UI state singleton from `webui/utils/state.py`.

sections.title: Resolve the recommended action
sections.explanation: `execute_trade_after_analysis` exits early if the symbol has no state or the analysis is not complete. It looks for a typed `final_trade_intent` in three places (symbol state, analysis results, full final state), and a typed action overrides the stored `recommended_action`. Only when neither exists does it fall back to parsing the final decision text using the trading or investment mode. If no action can be found, nothing is traded.

sections.title: Portfolio and regime sizing
sections.explanation: Two deterministic layers adjust the dollar amount without changing the direction. The portfolio layer (`adjust_new_position_notional`) applies correlation, volatility and gross-exposure limits from live Alpaca data; if it raises, new exposure (BUY/LONG/SHORT) is set to zero, so the system fails closed. The regime layer can only shrink BUY/LONG sizes, and its failures leave the amount unchanged, so it fails open because it can only reduce risk anyway.

sections.title: Strict position check
sections.explanation: The current position is read with `strict=True`. As the comment explains, treating a broker outage as NEUTRAL could re-buy an existing holding on each loop iteration or skip an exit, so any error aborts the trade and records the reason in `trading_results` for the UI.

sections.title: Order execution and reporting
sections.explanation: Typed intents go through `AlpacaUtils.execute_trade_intent`, optionally with risk-sizing parameters from config; older runs use `execute_trading_action` with the plain signal. Per-action results are split into successes and failures, intent warnings are logged, and the outcome is stored in `state['trading_results']`. On success, `signal_trade_occurred` flags the Alpaca panels for refresh. An outer `except` makes sure an unexpected error is recorded in state rather than crashing the analysis thread.

sections.title: run_analysis setup
sections.explanation: Computes the trade date in UTC for crypto pairs (symbols containing `/`) and in New York time otherwise, marks the symbol as running, and normalizes research depth from either the new dict form or the legacy integer. It copies UI choices (models, provider, language, shorts, checkpointing, extra provider settings) into the config, builds `TradingAgentsGraph`, resolves earlier memory-log outcomes, creates the initial state, and starts an audit run with an initial snapshot.

sections.title: Streaming the graph
sections.explanation: The compiled graph is streamed chunk by chunk; each chunk is appended to a trace, passed to `app_state.process_chunk_updates`, and sets `needs_ui_update` so polling callbacks redraw. An optional progress callback gets a completed-agent ratio, and a 0.1 s sleep throttles updates. The checkpointer context returned by `_graph_for_run` is exited in a `finally` block so the checkpoint store is closed even if streaming fails.

sections.title: Finalize, log, and auto-trade
sections.explanation: The last chunk is treated as the final state. The decision comes from the typed intent, falling back to `process_signal` on the text. The run is logged, a UI runtime snapshot (prompts, tool calls, counts) is written to the audit log, the decision is stored in the memory log for later reflection, and the checkpoint is cleared after a successful run. The UI state gets the decision, completed statuses, results and a fresh chart, and only if `app_state.trade_enabled` is set does it call `execute_trade_after_analysis`.

sections.title: Error handling and cleanup
sections.explanation: Any exception is printed, and if an audit run was started it is closed with status `failed` and the error message, so failed runs still appear in the audit trail. The progress bar is completed on failure. The `finally` block always clears `analysis_running`. Watch out: the `finally` assumes `current_state` is a dict, so the early `return` for a missing symbol state (where `current_state` is `None`), or a failure before it is assigned, would raise from inside `finally`.

sections.title: start_analysis entry point
sections.explanation: Called by UI callbacks. It first asks the safety guard whether the daily LLM budget allows another run and returns the refusal reasons if not; guard errors are ignored so a missing safety module does not block analysis. It converts analyst checkboxes into a list (requiring at least one), maps Shallow/Medium/Deep to 1/3/5 debate rounds while keeping the label for LLM parameter mapping, draws an initial chart, then runs the analysis synchronously and returns a status message.

webui/layout.py.overview: Assembles the full Dash component tree for the web UI. It creates the polling intervals and client-side stores, builds each panel from `webui/components/*`, and arranges them into a header, connection and safety panels, and four workspace tabs (Analysis, Portfolio, Reports, Performance). `webui/app_dash.py` calls `create_main_layout` once at startup.

sections.title: Panel imports
sections.explanation: Each UI area lives in its own component module (header, config, status, chart, decision, reports, backtest, Alpaca account, safety, cost, API config modal, connection), and this file only composes them. `REFRESH_INTERVALS` provides the polling periods.

sections.title: Refresh intervals
sections.explanation: Three `dcc.Interval` timers drive polling-based updates. The fast and medium intervals start disabled and are enabled by callbacks only while an analysis runs, so an idle dashboard does not poll constantly. The slow interval is always on so account data stays current. Because analysis runs on background threads and writes to `app_state`, these timers are how the browser picks up new state.

sections.title: Client stores and footer
sections.explanation: `create_stores` adds an app store, a chart store with default period `1y`, and two stores from `webui.utils.storage` for persisted settings and API keys, imported locally to avoid loading storage at module import. The footer offers a manual Refresh status button.

sections.title: Build panels
sections.explanation: `create_main_layout` instantiates every panel and wraps the Alpaca account section in a card, plus the API configuration modal.

sections.title: Prompt-modal bridge script
sections.explanation: An inline `html.Script` listens for `postMessage` events of type `showPrompt`, which embedded report iframes send, and clicks the matching `show-prompt-*` button by id or by its Dash props, so a normal Dash callback opens the prompt modal. If no match is found it clicks any prompt button and sets the modal title directly. Note that React-rendered `html.Script` elements are generally not executed by browsers, so this bridge may depend on how the page is rendered.

sections.title: Workspace tabs and shell
sections.explanation: The main content stacks the header, connection panel and safety panel above `dbc.Tabs`. As the comment notes, Bootstrap tabs keep every panel mounted, so callbacks bound to hidden components keep working and form inputs keep their values when switching tabs. The Analysis tab groups configuration with the status, chart and decision monitors; Performance combines backtest and LLM-cost panels. The fluid container uses the `app-shell` class for styling.

webui/utils/state.py.overview: Defines `AppState`, the in-memory, process-wide state shared by Dash callbacks and background analysis threads, and the `app_state` singleton. It tracks the symbol queue, per-symbol agent statuses, reports and prompts, LLM and tool call logs, loop and market-hour scheduling flags, and trading settings. Its central method `process_chunk_updates` turns streamed LangGraph chunks into UI-ready reports and status transitions, as described in the Dash Web UI tour step.

sections.title: Constructor fields
sections.explanation: Initializes queue and per-symbol storage, the split between `current_symbol` (shown in the UI) and `analyzing_symbol` (being processed in the background), counters, call logs, and loop, market-hour and trading settings. Several fields are assigned twice (loop, market-hour, trade settings, `session_start_time`), which looks like code added over time; the second assignments win but use the same values. State is plain Python objects with no locking, relying on simple assignments from threads.

sections.title: LLM call registration
sections.explanation: `register_llm_call` is called by the LLM layer with model, latency, sizes, usage and status. It appends a tagged tuple to `llm_calls_log`, recomputes the count, flags a UI update, and forwards the same payload to the run audit logger. Audit failures are swallowed so telemetry never breaks an analysis.

sections.title: Queue and symbol lookup
sections.explanation: `get_next_symbol` pops the next ticker, sets it as `analyzing_symbol`, and either initializes its state or starts a new session for it. It only sets `current_symbol` when nothing is displayed yet, so a user browsing one symbol's page is not moved when the next symbol starts. Small getters return the state for a symbol, for the displayed symbol, or for the analyzing symbol.

sections.title: Per-symbol state schema
sections.explanation: `init_symbol_state` defines the per-symbol dictionary the UI reads: 13 agent statuses (all `pending`), report slots and matching prompt slots, debate state, completion flags, decision fields (`recommended_action`, `final_trade_intent`), chart data, and a short session id. Fixing this schema in one place lets panels read keys without existence checks.

sections.title: Status, prompts, and reset
sections.explanation: `update_agent_status` defaults to the analyzing symbol, accepts only `pending`/`in_progress`/`completed`, and sets the UI flag only when the status actually changes. Prompt store and get helpers record the prompt behind each report for the prompt modal. `reset` clears everything for a fresh multi-symbol run.

sections.title: Tool call display and filtering
sections.explanation: `get_tool_calls_for_display` normalizes tool call log entries: dict entries are used as is, older tuples are converted with placeholder fields, and anything else becomes an error row. It then filters by agent, using substring checks plus the `_matches_agent_type` alias table that maps report keys to agent names, and by symbol, case-insensitively.

sections.title: Loop and session control
sections.explanation: `reset_for_loop` clears reports, prompts and statuses for each symbol but keeps the symbol entries, chart data and period so pagination still works between loop iterations, and gives each symbol a new session. Start and stop helpers set loop and market-hour flags that the scheduler threads read. `signal_trade_occurred` marks Alpaca data for refresh, `update_reports_count` counts non-empty reports, and `is_all_symbols_complete` checks the loop symbols.

sections.title: Analyst report ingestion
sections.explanation: `process_chunk_updates` targets the analyzing symbol, or the displayed one as a fallback, and builds an analyst order filtered by `active_analysts`. For each analyst report in a chunk it skips empty and recently repeated content, and once an analyst is completed it accepts only replacements at least 20% longer, so partial streaming output does not replace a finished report. It also caps update counts. Analysts move from `in_progress` to `completed` when their report arrives and then start the next pending analyst, which gives the UI a sequential progress display.

sections.title: Debate, trader, and risk updates
sections.explanation: Investment debate chunks set Bull and Bear researchers to in progress and show their latest messages, and a judge decision fills the research manager report and investment plan. The trader plan and typed `final_trade_intent` are copied when present. In the risk debate, each analyst's response is shown without its name prefix; when the judge decides, missing individual reports are filled from history, all risk agents and the Portfolio Manager are marked completed, the final decision and intent are stored, and `analysis_complete` is set.

sections.title: Message tracking and singleton
sections.explanation: Messages in a chunk are added to the LLM log as Reasoning or System entries. The displayed count prefers explicit `LLM_CALL` registrations and only uses message counts when none exist; tool calls are counted elsewhere, in `agent_utils`' timing wrapper. The first human message starts the first pending analyst if no analyst is running. The module ends by creating the shared `app_state` instance that all callbacks and threads import.

.github/workflows/tests.yml.overview: GitHub Actions workflow that runs the offline pytest suite on Python 3.11 and 3.12 and, in a separate job, lints the Postman collections and checks a locally running app instance. It is the CI part of the Deployment, CI and API Checks tour step, and makes sure tests pass without API keys.

sections.title: Triggers and policy
sections.explanation: Runs on pushes to `main`, on every pull request, and on manual dispatch. The token has read-only `contents` permission, and the concurrency group cancels older runs for the same ref so only the newest commit is tested.

sections.title: pytest matrix job
sections.explanation: Tests both supported Python versions with `fail-fast: false`, so one version failing does not hide results from the other. It caches pip, installs `requirements.txt` plus pytest, and runs `python -m pytest tests/`. As the comment explains, `python -m` puts the repository root on `sys.path` because the project is not installed, and no secrets are set so the suite must stay offline.

sections.title: postman job
sections.explanation: Installs a pinned `postman-cli@1.77.0` and Python dependencies, lints the maintained collections and environment with `scripts/check_apis.py lint`, then runs `tests/test_postman_checks.py`, which checks the App collection against an isolated running app. Live provider checks are left out on purpose, as the Postman README explains.

Dockerfile.overview: Multi-stage container build for the Dash web UI. A builder stage compiles dependencies into a virtualenv, and a slim runtime stage copies that virtualenv, runs as a non-root user, sets data paths to writable directories, and adds a health check. It belongs to the Deployment step of the tour and is used by `docker-compose.yml`.

sections.title: Builder stage
sections.explanation: Uses the BuildKit syntax directive and `python:3.11-slim-bookworm`. Compilers and XML/FFI headers are installed only here so that native wheels can build, then dependencies are installed into `/opt/venv`. Copying only `requirements.txt` before installing means the dependency layer stays cached when only source code changes.

sections.title: Runtime environment
sections.explanation: A fresh slim image gets the same Python settings plus `PORT`, `SERVER_NAME=0.0.0.0` (required for access from outside the container), and the `TRADINGAGENTS_*` paths for cache, results and memory log, so all state goes to known directories that can be mounted as volumes. Matplotlib's config dir points to `/tmp`. Only runtime libraries are installed (CA certificates, `libgomp1`, libxml2/libxslt, tzdata).

sections.title: Copy code and drop root
sections.explanation: The prebuilt virtualenv and source are copied in, the project is installed editable without dependencies, a system user `app` with a nologin shell is created, data directories are created and given to that user, and the container switches to `USER app`.

sections.title: Health check and command
sections.explanation: Exposes 7860 and adds a health check that requests the local UI with Python's `urllib` (no curl needed in the image), with a 45 s start period for app startup. The shell-form `CMD` uses `exec` so Python becomes PID 1 and receives stop signals, and passes `SERVER_NAME` and `PORT` to `run_webui_dash.py`.

docker-compose.yml.overview: Single-service Compose file that builds the Dockerfile and runs the web UI with environment variables from a `.env` file, a loopback-only port mapping, and named volumes for caches, results and trading memory. It is the recommended local deployment described in the Deployment step of the tour.

sections.title: Build, env, and runtime settings
sections.explanation: Builds the local Dockerfile into a named image. `init: true` adds an init process that forwards signals and cleans up child processes, which helps with the app's background threads. Secrets come from `${ENV_FILE:-.env}`, so a different file can be chosen without editing the Compose file, and the explicit `environment` entries set port, bind address, time zone (New York by default, matching US market hours) and data paths to match the image.

sections.title: Port, restart, and volumes
sections.explanation: The port is published on `127.0.0.1` only, so the dashboard, which can place orders, is not exposed on the LAN by default; `HOST_PORT` changes the host side. `restart: unless-stopped` and a 30 s stop grace period allow in-flight work to finish, and three volumes keep the data cache, evaluation results and `.tradingagents` state across container rebuilds.

sections.title: Named volumes
sections.explanation: Declares the three Docker-managed volumes used above. Named volumes avoid host permission problems with the non-root `app` user from the Dockerfile.

postman/README.md.overview: Documentation for the project's API checks: two Postman v3 YAML collections, one for the running app and one for external providers, plus how to run them with `scripts/check_apis.py` or the Postman app. It also sets the rules for credentials, the meaning of exit codes, and what CI covers. This is the API checks part of the tour's final step, and it follows the repository rule that provider checks stay read-only.

sections.title: Scope and collection table
sections.explanation: States that requests are kept only as editable YAML, with no duplicate JSON export, and lists what each collection checks: the app's HTML, controls and callback registration, and read-only checks for AI catalogs, the Alpaca account and bars, Finnhub, FRED, CryptoCompare, FXMacroData and Alpha Vantage.

sections.title: Running from the repository
sections.explanation: Shows the pinned CLI install and the `lint`, `app` and `providers` subcommands. Credentials come from the desktop app's `.env`, then the repository `.env`, with process environment values taking priority; selected services with missing credentials fail early. Provider names match the app, local servers use a separate optional key so remote keys are not sent to them, and the text notes that a catalog check does not prove inference works.

sections.title: Using the Postman app
sections.explanation: Explains how to use the shared workspace environment, where missing keys produce SKIPPED messages that do not count as passes. It sets credential rules: shared values stay empty, keys are never shared or pasted into URLs, and the CLI runner uses a temporary, redacted environment outside the repository.

sections.title: Results, CI, and maintenance
sections.explanation: Defines exit codes 0, 1 and 2 and the git-ignored redacted reports, and states that no orders, settings changes or paid inference are triggered. CI lints and runs only the App collection, so provider outages do not decide pull-request results, and order-failure behavior stays in the Python tests. Sync rules (create/update only, never force deletion) and links to the provider API references follow.

One-line system intro for the multi-timeframe technical analyst used when a deterministic JSON Technical Brief (1h/4h/1d) is supplied.

System prompt for the swing-trading news analyst, focusing on multi-day catalysts, sentiment trends, event calendars, and momentum drivers for {ticker}.
Prompt template that turns the social media and sentiment analysis for {ticker} into a final swing-trading BUY/HOLD/SELL proposal.
System prompt for the swing-trading social media analyst covering sentiment trends, influencer catalysts, retail positioning, and buzz persistence over 2-10 day holds.

System prompt for the expert reflection analyst that judges whether past trading decisions were correct, analyzes contributing factors, and distills improvements and lessons for memory.
